question: Universal Containers wants Case Status to automatically change to 'Escalated' whenever a Case sits in 'New' for more than 4 business hours, and a manager should get a mobile notification. The admin proposes a Workflow Rule with a time-dependent action. What should you point out?
options: Workflow Rules are the correct tool and nothing needs to change
Use Flow Builder (Scheduled Paths) instead of legacy Workflow Rules
This requires Apex because Workflow Rules cannot evaluate time
This requires a Process Builder process, since Flow cannot send mobile notifications
explanation: Time-based, declarative escalation logic is achievable without code, but Salesforce's strategic direction is Flow Builder (using Scheduled Paths) rather than legacy Workflow Rules or Process Builder — a common trap is assuming the old tool is still the 'correct' answer just because it can technically do the job.

question: A callout to an external shipping API must run synchronously while a user is still on the record page, with custom logic to retry on a specific HTTP error code before showing a friendly message. Which statement is correct?
options: A Flow's HTTP Callout action alone can handle all retry logic without any Apex
This scenario's custom retry/error-branching logic exceeds what's practical declaratively
This must be built entirely with Visualforce and cannot use Flow at all
Outbound Messages are the correct synchronous solution here
explanation: Flow can make external callouts, but intricate conditional retry logic based on specific error codes goes beyond typical declarative capability — the App Builder should recognize when to recommend a programmatic (Apex) component invoked from Flow, rather than forcing everything into pure clicks.

question: An admin built a validation rule, a roll-up summary, and 3 record-triggered flows on Opportunity, and performance has degraded. A colleague says the fix must be to 'convert everything to Apex' since declarative tools don't scale. Is this correct?
options: Yes, declarative automation always performs worse than Apex at any volume
No — the real issue is likely too many uncoordinated automations firing on the same object/event
Yes, but only because roll-up summary fields are deprecated
No, because Apex cannot run on Opportunity at all
explanation: A classic trap is assuming any performance problem justifies scrapping declarative tools for Apex. Best practice is first to consolidate and streamline automation (e.g., fewer record-triggered flows per object, correct order of execution) — moving to code isn't automatically the right fix.

question: A partner has published an Agentforce agent template on AgentExchange for warranty claim triage. The admin installs it and finds it references a custom object that doesn't exist in their org. What is the MOST accurate statement?
options: This means the AgentExchange listing is broken and should be reported as non-functional
AgentExchange templates often expect certain supporting metadata (objects, fields
AgentExchange only distributes agents that require zero configuration by definition
This confirms the agent must have been built exclusively for Data Cloud orgs
explanation: A common trap is expecting AgentExchange listings to work with zero setup. Most templates require some org-specific configuration (mapping fields/objects, permissions) before they're usable — installing isn't the same as being production-ready out of the box.

question: Which statement about the relationship between AgentExchange and AppExchange is MOST accurate?
options: They are the exact same marketplace with different names
AgentExchange is a distinct, purpose-built marketplace for Agentforce agents, topics
AgentExchange only allows free listings, while AppExchange only allows paid listings
AgentExchange replaced AppExchange entirely in the Summer '26 release
explanation: A common trap is treating the two marketplaces as interchangeable. AgentExchange is specifically scoped to Agentforce building blocks, while AppExchange is the long-standing general marketplace — knowing the distinction matters for scenario questions about 'where would you look for X'.

question: True or False: because an agent template comes from AgentExchange, it automatically respects the installing org's existing sharing rules and field-level security without any additional review.
options: True — Agentforce always operates strictly within the running user's existing permissions with no configuration needed
Partially true with a trap: while Agentforce actions generally do respect the running user's access by default
False — Agentforce completely bypasses all sharing model enforcement by design
False — Agentforce requires 'Modify All Data' for every user before it can function
explanation: The trap here is the absolute wording 'automatically... without any additional review.' Agentforce generally respects the running user's sharing/FLS, but agent-specific configuration can influence effective access, so admins should still verify behavior rather than assume zero review is needed.

question: OWD for a custom object 'Vendor Contract' is Private. A Permission Set grants 'View All' on Vendor Contract to the Finance team. A Sharing Rule ALSO shares all Vendor Contract records owned by the 'Legal' role with 'Read Only' to Finance. What access does a Finance user actually have?
options: Read Only, because the Sharing Rule is more specific and overrides the Permission Set
Full view access to all Vendor Contract records (View All from the Permission Set is broader and is not restricted by an unrelated
No access, because Private OWD blocks the Permission Set from applying
Edit access, because Sharing Rules always grant the highest level found among all rules
explanation: A common trap is assuming that a specifically-scoped Sharing Rule 'wins' over a broader permission. In reality, access is additive — the highest level of access from ANY source (here, 'View All' from the Permission Set) governs what the user can see, regardless of a narrower Sharing Rule also being in place.

question: A profile has Field-Level Security set to 'Read-Only' on the Discount_Percent__c field, but the field is also included as an editable field on a Quick Action layout the user can access. Can the user edit the field via the Quick Action?
options: Yes, because Quick Action layouts always override Field-Level Security
No — Field-Level Security is enforced everywhere, including Quick Actions, Flows, and APIs
Yes, but only in Lightning Experience, not Classic
No, but only because Quick Actions cannot contain custom fields at all
explanation: A frequent trap is assuming a UI element (like a Quick Action layout) can bypass Field-Level Security. FLS is a hard, platform-wide restriction — no page layout, quick action, or standard UI can override it.

question: A support rep profile has 'Read' but not 'Edit' on the Case object. The rep is added to a Public Group referenced by a Sharing Rule granting 'Read/Write' access to Cases owned by the support queue. Can the rep now edit those Cases?
options: Yes, the Sharing Rule's Read/Write grants edit access to those specific records
No — object-level permissions from the Profile/Permission Set act as a ceiling
Yes, but only if the rep is also the record owner
No, because Public Groups cannot be referenced in Sharing Rules for Cases
explanation: This is a classic trap: sharing rules control WHICH records are visible/editable, but the Profile/Permission Set's object-level CRUD permissions set the ceiling on WHAT the user can do at all. Without object-level Edit permission, no amount of record sharing grants edit access.

question: Which combination of features would correctly prevent a Sales rep from ever seeing Opportunities in the 'Legal Review' record type, even though their profile grants 'View All' on Opportunity?
options: Field-Level Security on the Record Type field
A Restriction Rule scoped to exclude that record type
A Sharing Rule with a 'Private' setting
Removing the Opportunity tab from their Lightning App
explanation: A tempting trap is Field-Level Security on 'Record Type' (not a real lockable field permission this way) or a Sharing Rule (which can only widen, not restrict). Restriction Rules are specifically designed to narrow visibility even on top of broad object permissions like View All.

question: A company's Role Hierarchy has Regional Manager above Sales Rep. OWD for Opportunity is Private. The admin wants Sales Reps to see each other's Opportunities within the SAME region, but Regional Managers should NOT automatically see reps' Opportunities (managers only need visibility into their own deals). What is the correct approach?
options: Do nothing — the Role Hierarchy already grants this by default
Use Sharing Rules based on a Public Group (per region) rather than relying on Role Hierarchy
Set OWD to Public Read/Write for Opportunity
Use Manual Sharing for every Opportunity individually
explanation: The trap is assuming Role Hierarchy is always the right tool for peer-to-peer sharing — it actually grants access UPWARD to managers by default, which is explicitly NOT wanted here. Public-Group-based Sharing Rules let peers share with each other without automatically cascading visibility to managers the way hierarchy-based access would.

question: A Sharing Rule is created to share all Accounts owned by the 'West' Public Group with 'Read Only' access to the 'East' Public Group. Later, OWD for Account is changed from Public Read Only to Private. What happens to the Sharing Rule?
options: It is automatically deleted because it's now redundant
It continues to function and becomes more meaningful
It becomes an error and blocks the OWD change
It automatically upgrades to Read/Write to compensate for the stricter OWD
explanation: A subtle trap is assuming that tightening OWD breaks or removes existing sharing rules. In fact, Sharing Rules exist precisely to grant access beyond whatever the OWD baseline is — tightening OWD makes such rules more relevant, not obsolete.

question: Universal Containers needs Opportunity access to align with a matrix of sales regions AND product lines simultaneously, where a rep might need access based on either dimension. Role Hierarchy reflects only the management chain. What is the BEST long-term solution?
options: Duplicate the Role Hierarchy to reflect regions and products separately
Implement Enterprise Territory Management
Create hundreds of individual Sharing Rules, one per rep
Set OWD to Public Read/Write to avoid the complexity
explanation: The trap is trying to force the Role Hierarchy (meant for management reporting lines) to also encode business dimensions like product line. Territory Management exists specifically to model these overlapping access needs cleanly.

question: A record owner manually shares a confidential Opportunity with a colleague using Manual Sharing, granting Read Only access. The Opportunity owner is later deactivated. What happens to that manual share?
options: It is automatically removed since manual shares depend on an active owner
It persists until explicitly removed or cleaned up manually
It automatically upgrades to Read/Write
It transfers automatically to the deactivated user's manager
explanation: A trap here is assuming user deactivation cleans up sharing automatically. Manual shares tied to records generally persist; admins must proactively manage record ownership/sharing when deactivating users.

question: A user builds a report using the standard 'Opportunities with Products' report type but can't find a custom field from a related custom object 'Contract Terms' that has a Lookup (not Master-Detail) relationship to Opportunity. What is the issue?
options: The field must be hidden via Field-Level Security
Standard report types don't automatically include fields from objects related via Lookup relationships
The user lacks 'Run Reports' permission
Reports cannot show data from any custom object
explanation: A common trap is assuming any related object's fields are automatically reportable. Standard/predefined report types only expose specific relationships; Lookup-related custom object data usually requires building a Custom Report Type to surface it.

question: A dashboard is set to run 'As Specified User' where that user is a System Administrator. Six months later, several users complain the dashboard suddenly shows far less data than before. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The dashboard type automatically degrades over time
The Administrator's own record access changed (e.g., role change, deactivated account, or reduced permissions)
Dashboards always lose data after 90 days by default
Reports feeding the dashboard were archived automatically
explanation: The trap is not realizing that a 'Run As specified user' dashboard is entirely dependent on THAT user's current access — if their access shrinks (role change, deactivation), everyone viewing the dashboard sees less, since it isn't dynamic per viewer.

question: A Sales Ops analyst wants a report showing Accounts that have NO related Opportunities created in the last 90 days, to flag at-risk accounts. Which reporting feature is specifically designed for this 'records without related records' scenario?
options: A standard filter on the Opportunity Created Date field
A Cross Filter (Accounts WITHOUT Opportunities, with sub-filter conditions on the Opportunity side)
A Bucket Field on Account
A Joined Report with two blocks
explanation: The trap is reaching for a normal filter, which can't express absence of related records. Cross Filters are purpose-built for 'has/doesn't have related records' logic, including sub-filtering the related object's criteria (like a date range).

question: Why might Bucket Fields be the WRONG choice when a sales manager wants Opportunity Amount ranges to be reusable across many different reports and dashboards org-wide, with consistent boundaries?
options: Bucket fields cannot categorize numeric data
Bucket Fields are defined per-report and are not centrally reusable/shared automatically across other reports
Bucket fields require Apex to configure
Bucket fields can only be used in dashboards, not reports
explanation: The trap is assuming Bucket Fields (built inside one specific report) automatically propagate everywhere. They're local to the report they were created in, so for enterprise-wide consistent categorization, a formula field or picklist is the more appropriate reusable solution.

question: A Joined Report combines an 'Opportunities' block and a 'Cases' block, both filtered to the same Account. A user asks why the totals in each block don't visually align in a single combined chart. What is the correct explanation?
options: Joined Reports always share one unified chart and this indicates a bug
Each block in a Joined Report is essentially an independent report grouped together for side-by-side comparison
Joined Reports cannot use different object types in different blocks
Cases can never appear in a Joined Report
explanation: The trap is expecting a Joined Report to automatically merge everything into one seamless dataset. It's designed for side-by-side comparison of otherwise separate report blocks — totals and default charts remain scoped per block unless deliberately configured otherwise.

question: A Permission Set Group bundles three Permission Sets, one of which explicitly denies 'Delete' on Contact via a muting permission set included in the group. A user's Profile separately grants 'Delete' on Contact. What is the user's resulting ability to delete Contacts?
options: They can delete Contacts, because Profile permissions always override Permission Set Groups
They cannot delete Contacts, since the muting permission set revokes that right
It depends on which was assigned first
Muting permission sets only affect field-level security, never object permissions
explanation: A subtle trap: normally permission sets only ADD permissions and can't take away what a profile grants — but Permission Set Groups support 'muting' permission sets specifically designed to revoke selected permissions within that group's combined effect, which is an exception worth knowing.

question: Which statement correctly describes how 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' interacts with a criteria-based Sharing Rule on a custom object?
options: It has no effect on custom objects and only applies to standard objects like Account
When enabled (the default and required setting for custom objects with Sharing Rules)
It always grants access downward to subordinates, never upward to managers
It can be selectively disabled per Sharing Rule but never at the object level
explanation: The trap is not realizing 'Grant Access Using Hierarchies' extends a sharing rule's access up the chain of command by default — and that some custom objects DO allow unchecking this at the object level, which is a nuance often tested.

question: A nonprofit wants a workflow where a Screen Flow guides volunteers through logging donations, then an approval step is needed only if the donation exceeds $10,000, with dynamic routing to whichever regional director owns the related Account. Which approach is correct?
options: This entire scenario cannot be done declaratively and requires a custom Apex approval engine
This is achievable fully declaratively: a Screen Flow for data capture
Only Process Builder (not Flow) supports triggering approval processes
Approval Processes cannot use dynamic, record-based routing and always require a hardcoded approver
explanation: The trap is assuming complexity (conditional approval + dynamic routing) automatically requires code. Both Screen Flows and Approval Processes support this declaratively, including dynamic approver determination based on related record data.

question: An admin wants to let an Agentforce agent installed from AgentExchange trigger an existing, tested Screen Flow when a customer requests a refund. What is required for this integration to work?
options: Nothing — all flows are automatically available as agent actions with no configuration
The Flow must typically be exposed/configured as an Action available to the agent (e.g.
The Flow must be rebuilt entirely inside Agentforce Builder and cannot be reused from Flow Builder
Screen Flows can never be invoked by an Agentforce agent, only autolaunched flows can
explanation: The trap is assuming any existing flow is automatically agent-ready. Flows generally need to be exposed as actions with the right type/configuration and permissions before an agent can invoke them — plus screen-based interaction has its own constraints in an agent context, requiring the right flow shape/action wrapper.

question: A custom object has OWD set to 'Controlled by Parent.' What determines a user's access to child records of this object?
options: The child object's own independent OWD setting, ignoring the parent entirely
The user's access to the PARENT record entirely determines access to the child record
Whichever is more permissive between parent and child OWD
This setting is only valid for Lookup relationships, never Master-Detail
explanation: The trap is thinking a 'Controlled by Parent' child object can have independent sharing behavior. Access is entirely inherited from the parent — a hallmark of Master-Detail detail objects — and you cannot create record-level sharing rules directly on that child object.

question: A regional VP needs a dashboard where EACH viewer sees only their own team's numbers, without the admin building a separate dashboard per region. The dashboard must also respect each viewer's individual record-level sharing. What is the correct setup?
options: A single static dashboard run as the VP, since the VP can see everything anyway
A Dynamic Dashboard set to run as the logged-in user
Multiple Joined Reports, one per region, run manually by the VP
A dashboard filter manually re-applied by each viewer every time they log in
explanation: The trap is over-engineering with duplicated static dashboards. A Dynamic Dashboard set to run as the viewing user automatically respects each person's own sharing/visibility — exactly the scenario described — without needing per-region copies.

question: A company wants Contacts to inherit the same sharing as their parent Account automatically, with no separate Contact-level sharing rules to maintain. Which native behavior/setting supports this most directly?
options: Manually replicate every Account sharing rule onto Contact as well
Set the Contact OWD to 'Controlled by Parent'
Set Contact OWD to Public Read/Write to simplify things
Use a Permission Set Group mirroring the Account's role hierarchy
explanation: The trap is assuming you must manually mirror every Account sharing rule onto Contact. 'Controlled by Parent' OWD is specifically designed so a child object's access automatically follows its parent's access — no duplicate rule-building needed.

question: An integration user's Profile has 'View All Data' system permission. Does this permission allow the integration user to see fields hidden from their profile via Field-Level Security?
options: Yes, 'View All Data' overrides Field-Level Security since it's a system-wide permission
No — 'View All Data' (and 'Modify All Data') grant access to ALL records regardless of sharing
Yes, but only for custom fields, not standard fields
No, because 'View All Data' only applies to reports, not direct record access
explanation: A classic trap is conflating record-level 'View All Data' with field-level access. Even the most powerful record-level permissions don't override Field-Level Security — FLS must be separately granted for the field to be visible at all.

question: Universal Containers tracks Purchase Orders, each with multiple Line Items. Line Items must be automatically deleted if the Purchase Order is deleted, and Line Item record access should always mirror the parent Purchase Order — no independent sharing needed. The admin proposes a Lookup relationship with a workflow rule to delete children when the parent is deleted. What is the issue?
options: There is no issue; this fully satisfies the requirement
Master-Detail already provides cascading delete and inherited sharing natively
Lookup relationships cannot have related lists, so this would fail entirely
Workflow Rules cannot delete records under any circumstance
explanation: The trap is over-engineering a Lookup + custom automation to replicate behavior that Master-Detail gives you for free (cascading delete + inherited sharing). When those exact behaviors are required, Master-Detail is virtually always the right native answer.

question: A recruiting object 'Interview' has a Master-Detail relationship to 'Job Application' as its only relationship. The business now also wants each Interview to independently roll up to 'Interviewer' (a Contact), with its own sharing rules distinct from the Job Application. What is the correct approach?
options: Change the existing Master-Detail to point to Interviewer instead
Add a second relationship as a Lookup to Interviewer instead of Master-Detail
This is impossible since an object can only have one relationship of any kind
Convert Job Application's relationship to Interview into a Lookup so both relationships can be Master-Detail
explanation: The trap is reflexively wanting Master-Detail for a new relationship. Here, since Interview needs sharing INDEPENDENT of Job Application, a Lookup relationship to Interviewer is correct — Master-Detail would tie sharing to Interviewer instead, breaking the required inheritance from Job Application.

question: A many-to-many relationship between 'Student' and 'Course' is implemented with a junction object 'Enrollment' using two Master-Detail relationships. The business now wants Enrollment records to be independently ownable and sharable, unrelated to either Student's or Course's sharing. What must change?
options: Nothing — Master-Detail junction objects can already be independently owned and shared
At least one of the Master-Detail relationships would need to become a Lookup
Add a third Master-Detail relationship to a dummy object to enable independent ownership
Change Enrollment's OWD to Public Read/Write to simulate independence
explanation: The trap is assuming junction objects with Master-Detail relationships can have independent sharing — they can't, by definition of Master-Detail (detail inherits sharing from master and has no OwnerId of its own historically for full master-detail). Achieving independent sharing requires converting to Lookup, with the tradeoff of losing native roll-up summaries from that side.

question: An object 'Employee' needs a self-referencing field so that each Employee record can reference their Manager, who is also an Employee. The admin wants roll-up summary counts of direct reports per manager. What relationship type should be used, and what is the catch?
options: A Hierarchical relationship field, since it's built for self-referencing manager relationships — BUT Hierarchical relationships are only available on the User object, not custom objects, so a self-referencing Lookup must be used instead on a custom object, and native roll-up summaries won't be available since it's a Lookup
A Master-Detail self-relationship, which is fully supported on any custom object
A Hierarchical relationship, freely available on any custom object including Employee
A Formula field referencing itself recursively
explanation: The trap is assuming Hierarchical relationships work on custom objects — they're exclusive to the User object. For a custom 'Employee' object, you'd need a self-referencing Lookup, which also means no native roll-up summary (roll-ups require Master-Detail), requiring a Flow/Apex-based count instead.

question: A company's data model has 'Warranty Claim' as a Master-Detail child of 'Product,' which is itself a Master-Detail child of 'Manufacturer.' The business wants a roll-up summary field on Manufacturer that sums Warranty Claim amounts directly, skipping the intermediate Product object. What must be true for this to work?
options: It works automatically since roll-up summaries traverse any number of Master-Detail levels by default
Roll-up summary fields only aggregate DIRECT children one level down
This requires converting all three objects into a single object
This is only possible using Data Cloud, not standard roll-up summaries
explanation: The trap is assuming roll-up summaries can skip a level. They only work one level (direct parent-child) at a time — multi-level aggregation requires a chain of intermediate roll-up fields, one per level, cascading the sum upward.

question: A Lookup relationship field 'Preferred_Vendor__c' on Purchase Order is changed to Required (not null) at the field level. Does this make the relationship behave like Master-Detail?
options: Yes, a Required Lookup is functionally identical to Master-Detail in every respect
No — making a Lookup field required only prevents blank values
Yes, but only for reporting purposes
No, but only because Required fields cannot be Lookups at all
explanation: The trap is conflating 'required' with 'Master-Detail behavior.' A required Lookup only enforces that a value must be present — it does not grant any of Master-Detail's structural behaviors like cascade delete, inherited sharing, or roll-up summary support.

question: An admin converts a Lookup relationship 'Account__c' on custom object 'Service Ticket' to Master-Detail so roll-up summaries can be used. What must be true of EVERY existing Service Ticket record before this conversion succeeds?
options: Nothing — Salesforce auto-populates a default Account for blank records
Every existing Service Ticket record must already have a non-blank value in the Account__c field
Only records created in the last 90 days need a value
The conversion works regardless, and blank records are simply hidden from reports afterward
explanation: The trap is assuming Salesforce will handle blank values automatically during the Lookup-to-Master-Detail conversion. In reality, every existing record needs a populated value first, since Master-Detail requires a parent on every detail record — this is a well-known pre-conversion checklist item.

question: Which statement about deleting a Master record when 'Field-level security' hides the Master-Detail relationship field from a user's profile is correct?
options: The user cannot delete the master record at all since they can't see the relationship field
Hiding the relationship field via FLS does not prevent cascading delete behavior if the user otherwise has delete permission on the master object
FLS on a Master-Detail field always blocks deletion of both master and detail
Cascading delete only applies if the relationship field is visible on the page layout
explanation: The trap is assuming FLS on the relationship field controls the cascade-delete mechanism. Cascading delete is a structural, platform-level behavior tied to the relationship type itself — hiding the field from view via FLS or page layout has no bearing on it.

question: A Number field with 2 decimal places storing prices needs to become a Currency field, since the business now operates in multiple currencies with multi-currency enabled. What should the admin expect?
options: A simple field type change with zero side effects
Multi-currency requires careful handling, not a simple type change
This conversion is impossible and requires deleting and recreating the field
Currency fields cannot have decimal places, so data will be truncated
explanation: The trap is treating a Number-to-Currency conversion as trivial. Once Advanced/multi-currency is involved, admins need to carefully consider how existing numeric values map to a currency and exchange rate — it's not just a cosmetic type change.

question: A picklist field 'Region' has record-type-specific picklist value sets (different available values per Record Type). The admin converts it to a Multi-Select Picklist to allow multiple regions per record. What commonly gets overlooked?
options: Multi-Select Picklists cannot be used in Record Types at all, so nothing needs review
Record-type-specific picklist value availability still applies, but any dependent picklist
Multi-select conversion automatically rewrites all dependent formulas
This conversion has no impact on Record Types or formulas whatsoever
explanation: The trap is underestimating the ripple effect: while record-type value restrictions still generally apply, everything built around a single-value assumption (ISPICKVAL-based formulas, certain validation rules) breaks once multiple values can be selected and stored as a delimited string.

question: A Text field storing free-form 'Customer ID' values from a legacy system needs to become an External ID for use in Data Loader upserts. The admin simply checks the 'External ID' checkbox on the existing field. Is anything else needed?
options: No, checking the box is sufficient for everything, including guaranteeing uniqueness
The admin should also strongly consider marking it as 'Unique' (case-sensitive or insensitive
External ID fields must always be Auto-Number, so this field type is invalid
This will automatically deduplicate any existing duplicate values already in the field
explanation: The trap is assuming 'External ID' automatically guarantees no duplicates. It enables upsert matching and indexing, but true uniqueness enforcement requires ALSO setting the 'Unique' attribute — otherwise duplicate values can still exist and cause ambiguous upsert matches.

question: Which scenario correctly identifies a case where changing a field's data type would cause SILENT data truncation rather than an outright blocked conversion?
options: Converting a Checkbox to a Picklist
Reducing a Text(255) field to Text(50) when existing values exceed 50 characters
Converting a Currency field to a Percent field
Converting a Lookup to a Master-Detail relationship
explanation: The trap is expecting the platform to always hard-block risky changes. Shrinking a Text field's max length is a case where existing data exceeding the new limit can be silently truncated — a well-known 'gotcha' admins must proactively check for before making the change.

question: A checkbox field 'Is_VIP__c' needs to be replaced with a Picklist ('VIP Tier: Gold/Silver/None') to support more granular tiering, while preserving historical TRUE/FALSE data as a starting point. What is the recommended migration approach?
options: Simply change the Checkbox field's type directly to Picklist in Setup
Create a new Picklist field and migrate the data with Flow or Data Loader
Rename the Checkbox field and Salesforce will auto-convert its type
Use Field-Level Security to add picklist values to the Checkbox field
explanation: The trap is expecting a direct in-place conversion for Checkbox-to-Picklist — that specific type change isn't directly supported, so the safe path is creating a new field and running a deliberate data migration/mapping step.

question: An admin needs to migrate 200,000 legacy Contact records into Salesforce, matching against existing Contacts by an external system ID to avoid duplicates, and some records reference Accounts that must be created if they don't already exist. Which tool and approach is correct?
options: The Data Import Wizard, since it supports Contacts and any volume of records
Data Loader using Upsert (with an External ID field for matching)
A single CSV import via the standard 'Import Contacts' button in Setup
Manual entry, since automation cannot handle conditional Account creation
explanation: The trap is defaulting to the simpler Data Import Wizard for what looks like a routine import. At 200,000 records with upsert-based deduplication logic, Data Loader (or an ETL tool) is required — the Wizard's volume ceiling and simpler UI-driven mapping make it unsuitable here.

question: A nightly integration needs Salesforce Opportunity data to always reflect the LATEST state of a legacy on-premise ERP system in real time, without storing a duplicate copy inside Salesforce or consuming Salesforce data storage. Which solution fits, and what is the key limitation to flag?
options: A nightly Data Loader batch job, which is the standard way to avoid storage use
Salesforce Connect using External Objects
A Scheduled Flow that fully re-imports all data every night
Big Objects, since they're designed specifically for real-time external system mirroring
explanation: The trap is picking External Objects/Salesforce Connect (correct choice for real-time, non-duplicated access) but forgetting to flag its real limitations — external objects have restricted support for standard relationship/automation features compared to native custom objects, which is often exactly what the exam probes.

question: During a Data Loader import of Opportunities with Master-Detail relationships to a custom parent object, several rows fail with a relationship resolution error even though the External ID values look correct in the CSV. What is a common overlooked cause?
options: Master-Detail relationships can never be populated via Data Loader under any circumstances
The External ID field on the parent object might not actually be marked as 'External ID' (or 'Unique')
The CSV file format is always the cause of such errors
This only happens when importing into Lookup relationships, never Master-Detail
explanation: The trap is assuming a value 'looking right' means the field is properly configured. If the target field isn't actually flagged as an External ID (or has case-sensitivity issues), Data Loader's relationship resolution will fail even though the raw values appear correct.

question: A company wants a full, downloadable backup of all Salesforce data (not just metadata) on a recurring basis, without any coding or third-party tools, primarily for compliance/audit archival, not active integration. What native feature satisfies this?
options: Change Sets, scheduled weekly
The Data Export Service in Setup, schedulable weekly or monthly
Salesforce Connect External Objects
Data Loader Extract configured as a one-time job only
explanation: The trap is confusing Change Sets (metadata only, not data) with data export needs, or assuming a manual one-time Data Loader extract satisfies a 'recurring, no-code' requirement. The native Data Export Service is purpose-built for scheduled, native data backups.

question: An admin runs a Data Loader UPDATE (not upsert) on 50,000 existing Case records to bulk-change a Status field, expecting existing automation (validation rules, flows) to behave exactly as manual UI edits would. What common surprise should they anticipate?
options: Data Loader always bypasses every validation rule and flow automatically
Depending on API version/settings and the specific automation type
Data Loader updates are always silently rejected if any automation exists on the object
Bulk updates via Data Loader can never trigger Flow automation under any circumstances
explanation: The trap is assuming bulk API-driven updates behave identically to one-off UI edits with no caveats. While most automation does fire the same way, badly bulkified automation can hit governor limits or cause unexpected side effects at scale — a real consideration before mass data updates.

question: A report needs to show Accounts alongside a rolled-up count of related Custom Object 'Support Plan' records, but 'Support Plan' relates to Account via a Lookup (not Master-Detail), and the business does not want to change the relationship type due to independent sharing needs on Support Plan. How can the count still appear reliably in reports?
options: It's impossible without converting to Master-Detail
Use a Custom Report Type joining Account and Support Plan (via the Lookup) for reporting purposes
Native roll-up summary fields work fine on Lookup relationships as long as a Custom Report Type also exists
Enable 'Roll-Up Summary Compatibility Mode' in Setup for Lookup relationships
explanation: The trap is thinking a Custom Report Type alone recreates roll-up summary functionality, or that some hidden setting enables roll-ups on Lookups. Since Support Plan needs independent sharing (ruling out Master-Detail), a Custom Report Type handles ad hoc reporting, while a Flow-calculated field is needed if the count itself must be a stored, queryable field on Account.

question: A 'Case' object has a Master-Detail relationship to a new custom object 'Escalation Log' (Case is master, Escalation Log is detail). Support agents complain they can no longer set a different OWNER for Escalation Log records than the related Case's owner. What is the correct explanation?
options: This is a bug that should be reported to Salesforce support
This is expected Master-Detail behavior, not a bug
Escalation Log must have an OwnerId field manually added via a custom field
Case must be converted to a Lookup relationship for this specific behavior to change, but this has no other implications
explanation: The trap is treating this as a bug rather than recognizing it as inherent Master-Detail behavior — detail records don't carry independent ownership; if independent ownership/sharing is truly required, the relationship needs to be a Lookup instead, with the tradeoff of losing cascade delete and native roll-up summaries.

question: Which of the following would MOST likely indicate that a many-to-many relationship should use a junction object with Master-Detail relationships, rather than simply adding two separate Lookup fields on one of the two objects?
options: The business needs each Student to relate to exactly one Course only
The pairing needs extra data captured, like a Grade per combination
The two objects will never have more than 10 records combined
One of the objects is a standard object like Account
explanation: The trap is not recognizing when a true many-to-many junction object is needed versus when a single Lookup would suffice. Needing to store per-pairing data (like a grade) and inherited sharing/cascade behavior signals a proper junction object with Master-Detail relationships is required, not just two separate Lookups.

question: A formula field of return type 'Checkbox' evaluates cross-object references three relationships deep to determine eligibility. Six months later, an intermediate relationship in that chain is deleted (the Lookup field itself is deleted). What happens to the formula field?
options: It continues to calculate correctly using cached historical values
The formula field will show an error or stop calculating correctly (often needing to be edited/fixed)
It automatically reroutes to the next closest relationship
Formula fields cannot reference relationships three levels deep in the first place, so this scenario is impossible
explanation: The trap is assuming formula fields are resilient to structural changes elsewhere in the data model. Deleting a relationship a cross-object formula depends on breaks that formula, requiring the admin to identify and fix (or remove) the now-invalid reference — a real-world data model change management concern.

question: An admin wants to prevent duplicate Account records during a large CSV import via Data Loader, using company legal name and country as the matching logic, but built-in Salesforce Duplicate Rules only run on UI-based saves in some configurations. What should the admin verify?
options: Duplicate Rules never apply to Data Loader imports under any circumstances, full stop
Whether the relevant Matching Rule and Duplicate Rule are configured to also run for the API/bulk context (not just standard UI actions)
Data Loader has its own separate, unrelated duplicate detection system that always takes priority
Duplicate Rules only work on Leads and Contacts, never Accounts
explanation: The trap is assuming duplicate rules always apply everywhere uniformly. Duplicate/Matching Rule configuration can be scoped, and admins need to verify the rule is actually set to evaluate in the context (API/bulk vs. UI) relevant to their import method — an easy detail to overlook.

question: Which situation BEST justifies choosing an External Object (via Salesforce Connect) over simply importing a nightly CSV snapshot of the same external data into a custom object?
options: When storage limits are not a concern and reporting speed is the only priority
When the business requires the Salesforce UI to always reflect the external system's CURRENT
When the external data will be edited primarily from within Salesforce
When Apex Trigger support on the object is a hard requirement
explanation: The trap is not weighing the real tradeoff: External Objects give live, non-duplicated data access but with meaningfully reduced platform feature support (automation, relationships). If real-time freshness matters more than that reduced feature set, External Objects are correct — if rich native automation is essential, a periodically-synced custom object may be more appropriate despite the staleness.

question: An object 'Shipment' has two Master-Detail relationships: one to 'Order' and one to 'Warehouse.' A user asks why they can't add a third Master-Detail relationship to 'Carrier.' What is the correct explanation?
options: There is a temporary bug and it should work after a metadata refresh
An object can have a maximum of 2 Master-Detail relationships as the detail side
Master-Detail relationships are limited to exactly 1 per object, so the second one to Warehouse was already invalid
Adding a third Master-Detail relationship requires a special license add-on
explanation: The trap is not knowing the hard limit: an object can be the detail side of at most 2 Master-Detail relationships. Any additional relationship needed beyond that must be implemented as a Lookup.

question: A Date field 'Contract_Start__c' needs to become a Date/Time field to also capture the exact signing time going forward. What happens to existing records' data during this conversion?
options: All existing values are permanently lost and fields reset to blank
Existing Date values are preserved and a default time component (typically midnight
The field must be deleted and manually recreated with no data carryover
This conversion is not permitted under any circumstances
explanation: The trap is assuming any type change wipes data. Date-to-DateTime is a supported, relatively low-risk conversion — existing dates are retained with an added (default) time component, unlike riskier conversions such as Picklist-to-Text.

question: A migration project needs to preserve original CreatedDate and CreatedById values from a legacy system when inserting historical records into Salesforce via Data Loader. What is required?
options: This is always possible by default with any Data Loader insert
This requires the 'Set Audit Fields upon Record Creation' permission (and enabling that feature)
CreatedDate can be set via Data Loader by default, but CreatedById cannot ever be changed
This is only possible via the Data Import Wizard, not Data Loader
explanation: The trap is assuming audit fields like CreatedDate are freely writable. They're normally system-managed; overriding them during data migration requires a specific permission ('Set Audit Fields upon Record Creation') to be enabled for the running user first.

question: A 'Case' object needs to track a many-to-many relationship with 'Product,' where each pairing also needs its own approval process and independent record-level sharing rules unrelated to either Case or Product's sharing. Why would a junction object using TWO Master-Detail relationships be the WRONG choice here?
options: Because junction objects cannot have approval processes
Because Master-Detail children cannot have independent OwnerId/sharing settings
Because Case and Product cannot be related via a junction object under any configuration
Because approval processes require Public Read/Write OWD
explanation: The trap is defaulting to 'junction = two Master-Details' as a rule with no exceptions. When independent sharing is a hard requirement (as it explicitly is here), Master-Detail is disqualified for that side, forcing a Lookup-based junction design instead.

question: Which pair of field type changes is generally considered LOW RISK (supported cleanly, minimal data impact) versus HIGH RISK (potential data loss or breakage) in Salesforce?
options: Low risk: Text to Long Text Area (increasing capacity)
Low risk: Picklist to Multi-Select Picklist with zero side effects; High risk: Number to Currency
Low risk: Auto-Number to Text; High risk: Date to Date/Time
Low risk: Checkbox to Picklist; High risk: Text to Long Text Area
explanation: The trap options pair up changes incorrectly. Expanding a Text field's capacity (or Text→Text Area) is low risk; removing a controlled picklist's structure by converting to Text is a well-known high-risk change because it breaks dependent picklists, validation, and reporting logic built on exact known values.

question: A company needs bidirectional, scheduled synchronization (not just one-way import) between Salesforce and an external HR system for Employee data, with transformation logic and error handling beyond simple field mapping. Which combination is MOST appropriate?
options: The Data Import Wizard scheduled to run nightly via a time-based workflow
A middleware/integration platform like MuleSoft
Salesforce Connect External Objects configured for write-back with no additional tooling
A single large Data Loader CSV export/import cron job with no additional tooling
explanation: The trap is trying to force basic tools (Data Loader, Import Wizard) to do a job they weren't designed for. Robust bidirectional sync with transformation/error-handling logic calls for proper middleware/integration tooling, not batch import utilities.

question: A formula field calculates Days_Open__c as TODAY() - CreatedDate on the Case object, intended to show how long a case has been open. Users report the field shows an error. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: TODAY() cannot be used in formula fields
CreatedDate is a Date/Time field, while TODAY() returns a Date
Days_Open__c must be a Text field, not a Number field
Case does not support formula fields referencing CreatedDate
explanation: The trap is not noticing the type mismatch: CreatedDate is Date/Time, but TODAY() is Date-only. Direct arithmetic between a Date and a Date/Time causes an error — DATEVALUE() must convert CreatedDate to a plain Date first.

question: A formula field on Opportunity must show a warning icon (via a Rich Text-like visual) when Probability is below 30%, but formula fields of type Text cannot render icons directly. What is the standard declarative approach?
options: This requires a custom Lightning Web Component with no declarative option
Use the IMAGE() function inside a Text formula field
Use a Roll-Up Summary field instead of a formula field
This is only possible using Conditional Highlighting on reports, not on the record itself
explanation: The trap is assuming visual indicators always require custom code. The IMAGE() function inside a formula field is a native, fully declarative way to conditionally show icons based on field values — a classic exam-style 'declarative capability' question.

question: A cross-object formula field on Contact displays the related Account's 'Annual_Revenue__c' custom field. For Contacts with no related Account (Account field blank), the formula throws an error instead of showing blank. What is the correct fix?
options: Cross-object formulas cannot reference custom fields on Account, only standard fields
Wrap the cross-object reference with BLANKVALUE() (or an ISBLANK() check) to gracefully handle the case where the related Account doesn't exist
Formula fields cannot be used on Contact at all
Convert the Account lookup to Master-Detail to fix the null-handling automatically
explanation: The trap is not anticipating null relationship references. When a lookup might be blank, cross-object formulas need explicit null-handling (BLANKVALUE/ISBLANK) — otherwise referencing a field through a nonexistent relationship can produce unexpected errors or blanks.

question: An admin builds a formula field using the PRIORVALUE() function to compare a field's current value to its value before the most recent save, intending to use it inside a plain formula field for a text summary shown on the page layout. What is wrong with this plan?
options: PRIORVALUE() does not exist in Salesforce formulas
There is no issue and this works perfectly in any formula field context
Formula fields cannot display text, so this is invalid regardless of function used
This requires a Roll-Up Summary field, not a formula field
explanation: This tests whether you can spot a fabricated function. PRIORVALUE() is not a real Salesforce formula function — change-detection style logic (like ISCHANGED) is only valid inside specific automation contexts (e.g., certain flow/validation contexts tied to record updates), not as a general-purpose formula field function.

question: A formula field needs to show 'Yes' if a currency field Amount__c is exactly evenly divisible by 500 (e.g., 1000, 1500, 2000), and 'No' otherwise. Which formula correctly achieves this?
options: IF(Amount__c / 500 = ROUND(Amount__c / 500, 0), "Yes", "No")
IF(MOD(Amount__c, 500) = 0, "Yes", "No")
IF(Amount__c > 500, "Yes", "No")
IF(TRUNCATE(Amount__c) = Amount__c, "Yes", "No")
explanation: The trap options look plausible (option A actually also works but is needlessly convoluted, while C and D are unrelated checks). MOD() is the clean, correct function for checking exact divisibility by testing if the remainder equals zero.

question: A roll-up summary field on 'Account' sums the Amount of related child 'Opportunity' records where Stage equals 'Closed Won,' using filter criteria on the roll-up field itself. A rep asks why an Opportunity that was Closed Won and then later had its Stage changed back to 'Negotiation' still seems to briefly reflect in historical reports as having counted. What is the correct explanation?
options: Roll-up summary fields cache values permanently and never update
The roll-up summary field itself recalculates immediately and correctly excludes the Opportunity once its Stage no longer matches 'Closed Won'
Filter criteria on roll-up summaries cannot reference Stage, a picklist field
This behavior indicates a bug requiring a Salesforce support case
explanation: The trap is confusing real-time roll-up recalculation (which does happen automatically and correctly) with static historical report snapshots (which don't retroactively update). The roll-up field is accurate NOW; old report exports simply reflect an earlier point in time.

question: The business wants a roll-up summary field on 'Opportunity' that counts related 'Quote' child records, but ALSO wants this same numeric value available as an input to a validation rule that blocks Opportunity submission if the count is zero. An admin says this isn't possible since roll-up summaries can't be referenced by validation rules. Is this correct?
options: Correct — roll-up summary fields are entirely invisible to validation rule formulas
Incorrect — validation rule formulas CAN reference roll-up summary field values directly
Correct, but only because Quote is a special protected object
Incorrect, but only if the roll-up field is converted to a formula field first
explanation: The trap is the false claim itself, stated confidently by a 'colleague' in the scenario — a pattern the real exam uses. Validation rules can absolutely reference roll-up summary fields like any other field; there's no such restriction.

question: An admin needs a roll-up summary field on 'Account' that shows the AVERAGE deal size of related Closed Won Opportunities. When building the roll-up, 'Average' isn't in the aggregate function dropdown. What is the correct declarative workaround?
options: This is impossible declaratively and requires Apex
Create two roll-up summary fields (SUM of Amount and COUNT of Opportunities under the same filter)
Use MAX and MIN together to approximate an average
Switch the roll-up field's data type to Percent, which unlocks the Average option
explanation: The trap is jumping straight to 'needs Apex' when a real, common declarative pattern exists: combine a SUM roll-up and a COUNT roll-up, then divide them in a formula field — a well-known workaround since native roll-ups don't support AVERAGE.

question: A roll-up summary COUNT field on 'Account' counts related 'Contact' records. The business now converts the Account-Contact relationship area to use 'Contacts to Multiple Accounts' (indirect relationships via the Account Contact Relationship object) for some Contacts. What happens to the original roll-up summary field?
options: It automatically recalculates to include both direct and indirect relationships seamlessly
It continues to count only DIRECTLY related Contacts (via the standard AccountId lookup on Contact)
It breaks entirely and must be deleted
It automatically converts into an indirect lookup rollup summary field with no admin action
explanation: The trap is assuming 'Contacts to Multiple Accounts' functionality is automatically reflected everywhere. A standard roll-up summary tied to the direct AccountId lookup won't pick up indirectly-related contacts through the separate Account Contact Relationship junction without extra configuration.

question: Why might a roll-up summary field configured with filter criteria 'Stage equals Closed Won' fail to update immediately when a related Opportunity's Stage changes via a Data Loader bulk update rather than the UI?
options: Roll-up summaries only recalculate for changes made through the standard UI, never through the API
This is a trap: the rule already fires correctly with OR() logic
Data Loader always bypasses roll-up summary recalculation by design
Filter criteria on roll-up summaries only evaluate during UI-based saves
explanation: This tests recognizing a false premise. Roll-up summaries recalculate on any DML, regardless of source (UI, API, Data Loader, Apex) — there's no special exemption for non-UI updates; the only nuance is potential processing delay at very large bulk volumes, not a categorical UI-only limitation.

question: A validation rule on Opportunity is: AND(ISPICKVAL(StageName, "Closed Won"), ISBLANK(Contract_Number__c)). The business wants this to ALSO allow existing Closed Won Opportunities (created before this rule existed) to be edited for unrelated fields without being forced to backfill Contract_Number__c. What change is needed?
options: Nothing — the rule already behaves this way by default
Add a condition that scopes the rule to only fire on the FIRST transition into Closed Won (e.g.
Delete the validation rule entirely since it can never work as intended
Add NOT(ISNEW()) to the rule, which will fix the issue
explanation: The trap is assuming the rule as written is already safe — as written, it will block EVERY future save of an existing Closed Won record missing a contract number, not just the initial transition. Scoping the rule to fire only when Stage is actively changing INTO Closed Won (not on every subsequent edit) is the correct fix; NOT(ISNEW()) alone doesn't solve this specific issue and is a distractor.

question: A validation rule references a Roll-Up Summary field to block saving an Opportunity if the roll-up (SUM of related Quote line amounts) doesn't match the Opportunity's own Amount field, within a tolerance. Users complain the validation rule sometimes fires unexpectedly for records where no related Quote exists at all. What is the likely issue?
options: Validation rules cannot reference roll-up summary fields, so this scenario is impossible
A SUM roll-up defaults to 0, not blank, with no related records
Roll-up summary fields must always be blank when no child records exist
This is expected correct behavior and no fix is needed
explanation: The trap is not accounting for a SUM roll-up summary's default behavior with zero related records — it typically evaluates to 0, not blank/null. Validation logic assuming the field is populated or blank (rather than potentially 0) can misfire; the formula needs to explicitly account for the no-children case.

question: A company needs a validation rule enforced ONLY for users in the 'Sales' profile, allowing 'Sales Ops' users to bypass it entirely when editing the same field. Which approach is correct?
options: Validation rules cannot be scoped by profile at all, so this requires Apex
Reference $Profile.Name or a custom permission inside the formula
Create two identical validation rules, one active and one inactive, and manually toggle them
Assign a Permission Set that disables validation rules for Sales Ops
explanation: The trap is assuming validation rules are all-or-nothing regardless of who's editing. You can reference $Profile.Name or (better practice) a Custom Permission via $Permission within the rule's formula to conditionally bypass the check for certain users — no Apex required, and there's no such thing as a permission set that 'disables' a specific validation rule directly.

question: A Flow performs an update to a Contact record's Email field as part of an automated data cleanup process. A validation rule on Contact requires a properly formatted email whenever Email is changed by an end user, but the Flow's cleanup logic sometimes intentionally sets a placeholder value that wouldn't pass that format check. What is the BEST approach?
options: Deactivate the validation rule permanently so the Flow can run
Have the Flow bypass validation via a specific 'bypass' mechanism (e.g.
Convert the validation rule into a Roll-Up Summary field
Grant the Flow's running user 'Modify All Data' so validation rules no longer apply
explanation: The trap is the blunt 'just deactivate it' or 'grant more permissions' approaches, which remove protection entirely rather than scoping the exception. The refined approach is building a deliberate bypass condition into the validation logic itself (often via a custom permission check) so only the intended automation context skips the rule.

question: A record-triggered Flow on Opportunity is configured to run 'Before Save' and includes an element that creates a related Task record. The Flow fails to activate with an error. What is the most likely cause?
options: Before-Save flows have a lower element limit than After-Save flows
Before-Save (fast field update) record-triggered flows can only update fields on the SAME record
Task cannot be created by any Flow, only by Apex
Before-Save flows cannot reference the Opportunity object at all
explanation: The trap is not knowing the precise capability boundary of Before-Save flows. They're optimized purely for updating the triggering record's own fields in memory — any action requiring separate DML (like creating a related Task) needs an After-Save flow instead.

question: A Screen Flow is embedded on a Lightning Record Page for Case. It includes a 'Get Records' element followed by a Decision element checking if the returned collection has more than one record, then a Loop. Users report the Decision always evaluates as if the collection is empty, even when multiple matching records clearly exist. What is the MOST likely root cause?
options: Loops cannot be used after Decision elements
The Get Records element is likely configured to return only the 'first record' (single record output) rather than a collection of multiple records
Decision elements cannot evaluate collection variables under any configuration
Screen Flows cannot use Get Records elements at all
explanation: The trap is a subtle configuration detail: Get Records has an option to store 'only the first record' vs. 'all records' as a collection. If mistakenly set to single-record mode, downstream logic expecting a multi-record collection will behave unexpectedly — exactly the kind of detail-oriented trap the real exam favors.

question: An Autolaunched Flow is invoked as a Subflow from a parent Record-Triggered Flow. The subflow contains a Screen element. What happens when this configuration is activated?
options: It works fine; the screen simply displays inline within the record-triggered flow's execution
This configuration is invalid in a record-triggered (background) context
The screen displays the next time the triggering user manually opens the record
Only the first Screen element in a Subflow is ignored while the rest of the subflow executes normally
explanation: The trap is assuming Screen elements can be safely embedded anywhere as long as they're wrapped in a Subflow. Record-triggered (background) flow contexts have no active UI session, so calling a Subflow that includes a Screen element in that context is invalid and will prevent proper activation/execution.

question: A Flow uses a Loop over a collection of 200 Opportunity records, and inside the loop, a 'Create Records' element inserts one Task per iteration (200 separate DML operations inside the loop). What is the correct best-practice concern here?
options: This is optimal and recommended Flow design for any volume
Performing DML (Create/Update/Delete Records elements) INSIDE a loop is a well-known anti-pattern
Loops in Flow are limited to 10 iterations maximum, so this scenario cannot occur
DML elements automatically bulkify themselves even when placed inside a loop, so there's no actual concern
explanation: The trap is not recognizing a classic Flow anti-pattern: DML inside a loop causes one DML operation per iteration, risking governor limits at scale. The correct, bulkified pattern collects records in a variable during the loop and performs a single Create/Update/Delete Records call after the loop completes.

question: An Opportunity Approval Process locks the record upon submission. A Flow later needs to update the SAME Opportunity's 'Last_Reviewed_Date__c' field while it's still pending approval, using an After-Save record-triggered Flow with elevated context. What should the admin expect?
options: Flows can never update locked records under any circumstances, even with elevated permissions
A locked record blocks edits from users without the 'Modify All Data' permission (or an approval-process-specific bypass) in the standard UI
Locked records can only be updated by the original submitter
Unlocking must always happen manually through Setup before any update succeeds
explanation: The trap is an absolute 'never' claim. Record locking primarily restricts standard user edits; depending on configuration (running context, specific field-update mechanisms tied to approval steps, or elevated permissions), certain automated updates to locked records ARE possible — the nuance is knowing it's configuration-dependent, not a blanket impossibility.

question: A multi-step Approval Process routes first to the submitter's manager, then to a 'Finance Approver' determined by a lookup field on the record. The Finance Approver field is blank on some records. What happens when those records are submitted and reach that step?
options: The approval automatically skips to the final approval action
The approval process would typically fail to route correctly at that step
The CEO automatically becomes the default approver on any org
The record becomes permanently locked with no way to resolve it
explanation: The trap is assuming the system automatically compensates (auto-skip, default to CEO). Dynamic approver routing based on a blank lookup will fail to route properly, which is why good design proactively enforces the field's population (validation rule) or provides a queue-based fallback rather than leaving it to chance.

question: An Approval Process's Final Rejection Action is configured to send an Email Alert and change Status to 'Rejected.' The business also wants an automatic Task created for the original submitter to revise and resubmit. The admin says Final Rejection Actions can only include Email Alerts and Field Updates, so a Task can't be created this way. Is this accurate?
options: Accurate — Approval Process actions are strictly limited to Email Alerts and Field Updates only
Not fully accurate — Approval Process actions can include Task creation (along with Field
Accurate, but only because Task creation requires Apex regardless of approval processes
Not accurate, but only because Outbound Messages can create Tasks indirectly
explanation: The trap is the admin's confident-but-wrong claim in the scenario. Standard Approval Process actions actually include Task creation, Field Updates, Email Alerts, and Outbound Messages — Task creation is natively supported, no Apex or workaround required.

question: A company needs Opportunities that haven't moved stage in 45 days to trigger a reminder, checked once per day, without any user interaction. A junior admin proposes a Record-Triggered Flow set to run 'every time a record is updated,' reasoning that this will re-check the 45-day condition continuously. What is wrong with this approach?
options: Record-triggered flows cannot check date-based conditions at all
A record-triggered flow only fires when the record is actually created/updated/deleted
Record-triggered flows automatically run daily in the background on all records regardless of edits
This requires Apex Scheduled classes since no declarative option monitors elapsed time
explanation: The trap is a common misunderstanding: record-triggered automation only fires on actual DML events, not the mere passage of time on an unedited record. Detecting 'nothing happened for 45 days' requires a Scheduled-Triggered Flow (or scheduled path) that actively queries for stale records on a timer.

question: A Platform Event is published whenever an external warehouse system marks an order as 'Shipped.' The business wants a Salesforce Flow to react and update the related Order's status within seconds. Which Flow type is correct, and what is a key constraint to flag?
options: A Scheduled-Triggered Flow running every minute, which is 'near real time' enough
A Platform Event-Triggered Flow, which is autolaunched and reacts to the event nearly immediately
A Screen Flow, since it can be manually triggered by a user upon seeing the event
A Before-Save Record-Triggered Flow on the Order object, since Platform Events are treated as Order record updates
explanation: The trap is picking a 'close enough' alternative (like a 1-minute scheduled flow) instead of the purpose-built Platform Event-Triggered Flow. The added nuance often missed is that such flows work from the event's payload data, not a existing Salesforce record context, so they must explicitly query/match the correct target record.

question: An admin builds a Before-Save record-triggered Flow on Lead intended to also send a follow-up email to the Lead's owner whenever the Lead Score exceeds 90. The flow fails to include the desired Send Email action in the available element list within that context. What is the explanation?
options: Send Email actions require a paid add-on license not enabled in this org
Before-Save flows are restricted to fast field updates on the triggering record only
Send Email actions can only be used in Screen Flows, never any autolaunched flow
The Lead object doesn't support email actions in any flow context
explanation: The trap is expecting a Before-Save flow to support the full range of Flow actions. Its scope is intentionally limited to updating the triggering record's own fields for performance reasons — anything else (emails, related record creation, etc.) requires an After-Save flow.

question: A business wants a fully declarative, multi-user, multi-stage business process (e.g., a loan approval spanning several departments each completing their own step over days), with visibility into where each case currently sits in the overall process. Which capability is BEST suited, especially considering it is now included at no additional cost as of Summer '26?
options: A single large Screen Flow with dozens of screens chained together
Flow Orchestration, which is purpose-built for coordinating multi-step
A single Approval Process with 25 sequential steps
A Scheduled-Triggered Flow polling for status changes every hour
explanation: The trap is defaulting to an oversized single Screen Flow or a chain of approval steps to force-fit a genuinely multi-stage, multi-user orchestrated process. Flow Orchestration exists specifically for this, and Summer '26 removed the cost barrier, which is a meaningful, current consideration for design recommendations.

question: Two record-triggered Flows exist on the same object, both set to run on record update, both 'Before Save.' One flow sets Field A based on Field B, and the other sets Field B based on Field A, creating a circular dependency. What tool should an admin use FIRST to diagnose and resolve the execution order and potential conflict?
options: Data Loader's dependency viewer
Flow Trigger Explorer
The standard Recycle Bin's audit trail
Schema Builder's relationship map
explanation: The trap is not knowing the specific tool designed for exactly this problem. Flow Trigger Explorer consolidates visibility into all triggered flows on an object and lets you reorder/inspect them — the direct answer for diagnosing multi-flow conflicts like circular field dependencies.

question: A Flow that previously worked correctly begins silently failing after a related picklist field had one of its values deactivated (not deleted) in Setup. The Flow's Decision element checks for that exact picklist value using ISPICKVAL-equivalent logic. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Deactivating a picklist value has no effect on existing automation referencing it
It only stops new records from getting that value going forward
Deactivating a picklist value automatically deletes the Decision element referencing it
This will cause the Flow to throw a runtime error every time it executes
explanation: The trap is assuming any related metadata change causes an outright Flow error. Here it's subtler — deactivating a picklist value just stops new assignment of that value, so logic keyed to it stops being triggered on new records, which can present as an automation 'not working' issue without any actual error being thrown.

question: An admin needs to understand exactly what changed between Flow Version 4 and Version 6 of a complex record-triggered Flow, including changes to a Transform element's field mappings, before deciding whether to roll back. Which Summer '26 capability directly addresses this?
options: Manually re-opening each version side by side with no dedicated comparison tooling, since none exists
The Flow version-comparison tool introduced in Summer '26
Deleting Version 5 to force Salesforce to auto-generate a diff report
Only Setup Audit Trail can show this level of detail
explanation: The trap is assuming there's no dedicated tool and resorting to manual comparison. Summer '26 introduced a built-in Flow version-comparison tool specifically to show differences (including transform mapping changes) between versions — directly relevant, current platform knowledge.

question: An Agentforce agent is configured with an Action that invokes an Autolaunched Flow to process refund requests. A customer's request fails partway through the Flow due to a validation rule blocking a status update. What should the App Builder expect regarding the agent's behavior?
options: The agent will always crash and become permanently unusable for that user
The agent's action will reflect the Flow's actual outcome (including failure due to the validation rule)
Agentforce automatically disables all validation rules for any action it invokes
The Flow will silently ignore the validation rule failure and report success regardless
explanation: The trap is assuming Agentforce operates outside or above existing declarative guardrails. It invokes the Flow like any other caller — existing validation rules still apply, and how gracefully a failure surfaces depends on proper fault path handling within the Flow itself, not some special agent bypass.

question: As of Summer '26, an admin wants to create a new Agentforce agent while actively building automation in Flow Builder, without switching to a separate tool. What capability supports this, and what related platform change should the admin be aware of?
options: Agents can only ever be created in the standalone Agentforce Builder; Flow Builder has no such integration
Flow Builder now allows selecting an Agent action to create an agent inline without tool-switching
This requires a separate paid Agentforce Studio license not related to Flow at all
Agent creation from Flow Builder was deprecated in Summer '26 in favor of Apex-only agent definitions
explanation: The trap is not knowing two related, current facts together: Flow Builder's inline agent-creation capability AND the broader platform shift where the New Agent button now opens only the new Agentforce Builder — both are genuinely new in this release window and could appear as linked exam-relevant trivia.

question: A formula field on Opportunity concatenates the Owner's name with the Account's Billing City using cross-object references: Owner.Name & ", " & Account.BillingCity. The field works for most records but errors for Opportunities where the Owner is a Queue rather than a User. What is the correct explanation?
options: Formula fields cannot reference the Owner field under any circumstances
Owner.Name may not resolve the same way when Owner is a Queue
Queues cannot own Opportunities in Salesforce
This is unrelated to Owner type and is actually caused by the Account reference
explanation: The trap is not recognizing that OwnerId is polymorphic (can point to a User OR a Queue on objects that support queue ownership). Fields that exist on User may not behave identically when the owner is actually a Queue, which is a subtle but real cross-object formula gotcha.

question: Which of the following correctly describes a limitation of formula fields that is commonly tested as a 'trap' answer choice?
options: Formula fields can trigger Time-Based Workflow actions directly, just like a date field change
Formula fields are recalculated in real time whenever displayed/queried and are NOT stored values in the database
Formula fields count against an object's field history tracking allocation identically to editable fields
Formula fields can be edited via Data Loader like any Text field
explanation: The trap options all describe things formula fields CANNOT actually do as if they could. Because formula fields are calculated on the fly rather than stored, they can't serve as literal time-based workflow triggers the way a real Date field can, and they're also not directly editable via Data Loader nor typically tracked in field history the same way stored fields are.

question: An Opportunity has a Master-Detail relationship to a child object 'Opportunity Milestone.' A roll-up summary field 'MAX(Milestone_Date__c)' is created on Opportunity. A user asks whether this roll-up will automatically exclude Milestones where Milestone_Date__c is blank. What is correct?
options: Blank date values are always treated as the lowest possible date and will never be selected by MAX
Roll-up summary fields (MIN/MAX) simply ignore records where the target field is blank when determining the min/max value
Blank values will cause the entire roll-up field to show an error
MAX roll-ups require the target field to be marked as Required, or the roll-up will not save
explanation: The trap is assuming blank fields are treated as some default value (like zero or lowest possible) in MIN/MAX calculations. In reality, roll-up summaries simply skip/ignore records where the relevant field is blank when computing MIN or MAX.

question: A validation rule uses the formula: OR(ISBLANK(Phone), ISBLANK(Email)), intended to require BOTH Phone and Email to be populated before saving a Contact. QA reports the rule sometimes doesn't fire when only Email is missing. What is the actual issue with this scenario as described?
options: This is a trap: validation rules only fire on save, never on delete
The formula needs to use AND() instead of OR() to work as intended
ISBLANK() cannot be used twice in the same formula
OR() only evaluates the first condition and ignores the second
explanation: This tests whether you can verify formula logic rather than assume the reported problem matches a plausible-sounding but wrong explanation. OR(ISBLANK(Phone), ISBLANK(Email)) is actually correct for requiring both fields — the real-world cause of the reported bug must lie elsewhere (rule scope/activation), which is the more likely explanation to investigate.

question: A validation rule needs to block deletion of any Opportunity in 'Closed Won' stage. An admin builds the validation rule formula ISPICKVAL(StageName, "Closed Won") and is confused why users can still delete Closed Won Opportunities. What is the correct explanation?
options: The formula syntax is wrong and should use StageName = "Closed Won" instead
Validation rules ONLY fire on record insert/update (save) operations
This works correctly and the reported issue must be a caching problem
Validation rules block deletion by default and this one is unnecessary
explanation: The trap is not knowing a fundamental scope limitation: validation rules only run on save (insert/update), never on delete. Blocking deletion requires a different tool entirely (e.g., a Flow with a delete trigger context, or careful permission/sharing design) — this is a frequently tested boundary.
