question: A Flow variable is defined as a 'Record Variable' of type Opportunity (not a collection). Later in the Flow, an element attempts to assign a list of five Opportunities (from a Get Records element configured to return multiple records) into this single record variable. What happens?
options: This works fine; the variable automatically becomes a collection to hold all five records
This causes a Flow error/build-time validation issue
Only the first of the five records is silently kept with no warning
The Flow will randomly select one of the five records at runtime with no error
explanation: The trap is not recognizing the fundamental distinction between a single Record Variable and a Record Collection Variable in Flow. Attempting to store multiple records in a single-record variable is a genuine type mismatch that Flow Builder should catch, not something that resolves 'automatically' or silently.

question: A record-triggered Flow's entry condition is set to fire 'only when a record is updated to meet the condition criteria,' checking Status__c = "Approved". A record is inserted directly with Status__c already set to "Approved" (never going through an update transition). Does the Flow fire?
options: Yes, because the condition matches regardless of whether it's a create or update
This depends on how entry criteria evaluation is scoped: if the Flow is configured to trigger on 'Create' as well as 'Update
Flows can never fire on record insert under any configuration
This always fires exactly once regardless of trigger type configured
explanation: The trap is oversimplifying entry condition + trigger type interactions. The exact behavior depends on whether the Flow is scoped to Create, Update, or both, and how the entry condition (which can require a change from not-meeting to meeting criteria) is evaluated — a nuance that's easy to get wrong if you assume 'the condition matches' is the only factor.

question: An After-Save record-triggered Flow on Contact updates a related Account field using an Update Records element, without any entry condition restricting re-entry. The Account has its own After-Save Flow that also updates a field on that same Contact whenever the Account changes. What risk does this configuration create?
options: No risk; Salesforce automatically prevents any circular automation between related objects
A recursive automation loop between the Contact and Account flows
This can only happen with Before-Save flows, never After-Save flows
This risk only applies to Apex triggers, not Flow-to-Flow interactions
explanation: The trap is assuming the platform automatically prevents recursive automation across objects. It doesn't — cross-object automation ping-ponging between two flows (or a flow and a trigger) is a real, well-known risk requiring deliberate entry conditions or recursion-control patterns to avoid hitting governor limits.

question: A Flow needs to send different email templates depending on the customer's Language field (5 possible values), and a developer suggests writing an Apex trigger since 'Flow can't handle multi-branch logic well.' Is this justified?
options: Yes, multi-branch conditional logic like this always requires Apex

No — a Decision element with multiple outcome paths (or a single Email Alert setup referencing a formula-selected template merge field) handles multi-branch conditional logic natively and declaratively
Yes, but only because email templates cannot be dynamically selected declaratively at all
No, but only if there are fewer than 3 possible values
explanation: The trap is the confidently wrong claim embedded in the scenario. Multi-branch conditional logic (like picking one of five email templates) is squarely within Flow Builder's native declarative capability via Decision elements — no Apex is needed here.

question: An approval process is configured with 'Allow submitters to recall approval requests' UNCHECKED. A submitter realizes they made an error immediately after submitting and wants to recall and resubmit at the correct data. What is the outcome?
options: They can always recall regardless of this setting, since recall is a universal user right
They cannot recall the request, since that setting was left unchecked
The approval process automatically allows recall after 24 hours regardless of the setting
This setting only affects reporting visibility, not actual recall functionality
explanation: The trap is assuming recall is always available to submitters by default. It's explicitly a configurable checkbox on the Approval Process — if unchecked, the submitter genuinely cannot self-service recall, and administrative intervention becomes necessary.

question: A company wants an Approval Process where the SAME approval request can be simultaneously reviewed by three different department heads, requiring UNANIMOUS approval before proceeding, rather than a strict sequential chain. Is this achievable declaratively?
options: No, Approval Processes only support strictly sequential, single-approver-at-a-time steps
Yes — Approval Processes support parallel approval steps (assigning multiple approvers on one step) with a configurable rule of 'Approve if ALL approvers approve' (unanimous)
No, unanimous multi-approver logic always requires a custom Apex approval framework
Yes, but only by creating three entirely separate, redundant Approval Processes run in sequence
explanation: The trap is assuming parallel/unanimous approval logic is too complex for declarative tools. Salesforce Approval Processes natively support parallel approval steps with configurable unanimous-vs-any-one-approver logic — a frequently underestimated built-in capability.

question: A Flow interview is shown as 'Paused' indefinitely in Setup's Paused and Failed Flow Interviews list, tied to a Wait element with no configured time-based resume condition ever being met. What is the most appropriate admin action?
options: Ignore it; paused flow interviews automatically resolve themselves after 30 days with no admin action needed
Investigate the Wait element's configured resume conditions
Delete the entire Flow definition immediately to clear the paused interview
Paused interviews cannot be viewed or managed by admins under any circumstances
explanation: The trap is either ignoring it (assuming auto-resolution that doesn't reliably happen for a fundamentally broken wait condition) or an overly drastic response (deleting the whole flow). The correct approach is targeted: diagnose the Wait condition logic, resolve the stuck interview, and fix the underlying flow design.

question: An admin wants to temporarily test a bug fix in a new Flow version without affecting users still actively relying on the currently active version, and without losing the ability to roll back instantly if the fix doesn't work. What is the correct practice?
options: Directly edit and save changes into the currently active version, since Flow doesn't support multiple versions
Create and activate a NEW version with the fix, keeping the previous version intact and inactive but available
Delete the current version entirely before creating the replacement
Clone the Flow into an entirely separate Flow with a different API name and manually redirect all triggering logic
explanation: The trap is not leveraging Flow's built-in versioning. Editing in place destroys the known-good version's isolation; the correct pattern is creating a new version (keeping the old one intact and available for instant rollback) rather than riskier alternatives like full deletion or unnecessary duplication into a separate Flow.

question: A company wants an Agentforce agent that can both answer general product questions (using retrieval-augmented generation over a knowledge base) AND execute a deterministic refund process via an existing Flow, choosing the right approach per customer request. What best describes how Topics and Actions relate to this scenario?
options: A single Action must handle both generative Q&A and the deterministic refund process together as one indivisible unit
Topics scope the agent's areas of expertise (e.g., 'Product Questions' vs. 'Refunds')
Topics and Actions are interchangeable terms for the same configuration concept
Deterministic processes like Flow-based refunds cannot be exposed as Agentforce Actions under any configuration
explanation: The trap is conflating Topics and Actions, or assuming deterministic Flow logic can't coexist with generative capabilities in the same agent. Topics organize scope, Actions are the executable units within that scope (including both knowledge retrieval and flow invocation), and the agent's reasoning selects among them per request — a foundational Agentforce architecture concept.

question: The business wants a roll-up summary field on Account that counts related Opportunities, but explicitly EXCLUDES Opportunities in a specific Record Type ('Internal Test'), while including all other record types. Is this achievable using roll-up summary filter criteria?
options: No, roll-up summary filter criteria cannot reference Record Type at all
Yes — roll-up summary field filter criteria can reference the Record Type field (e.g.
No, this requires a Flow-based rollup instead since Record Type is a protected system field
Yes, but only if the Record Type field is first converted to a custom picklist field
explanation: The trap is assuming Record Type is somehow off-limits for roll-up summary filtering because it's a 'system' concept. In practice, Record Type is filterable in roll-up summary criteria just like standard/custom picklists, making this a straightforward declarative solution.

question: A validation rule combines two conditions with AND() intending to require a Reason field ONLY when a checkbox 'Is_Exception__c' is TRUE, written as: AND(Is_Exception__c, ISBLANK(Reason__c)). A tester unchecks the checkbox and successfully saves with a blank Reason, then re-checks it later and is properly blocked until Reason is filled in. Is this validation rule working as intended?
options: No, this is a bug; the rule should always require Reason regardless of the checkbox
Yes, this is exactly the correct, intended behavior
No, ISBLANK() must be replaced with NOT(ISBLANK()) for correct behavior
Yes, but only by coincidence, since AND() with a checkbox never works reliably in production
explanation: This tests whether you can correctly validate WORKING logic rather than assume something is broken just because a scenario is described in detail. The AND() logic here is textbook-correct for a conditionally-required field, and the tester's described behavior is exactly the intended outcome — recognizing correct behavior is as important as spotting bugs.

question: A Screen Flow embedded on a Case record page needs to pre-populate a field with the current record's Case Number without the user typing it. What must be configured for this to work correctly?
options: Nothing; all Screen Flows automatically have full access to every field of the host record with no setup
The Flow needs a Record Id input variable available (automatically passed when embedded on a record page
This requires a custom Lightning Web Component wrapper around the Screen Flow
Case Number specifically cannot be referenced inside any Flow since it's an auto-number field
explanation: The trap is assuming a flow embedded on a record page magically has full access to that record's data with zero configuration. It needs an explicit Record Id variable (passed automatically by the Lightning page component under the right variable name) and a Get Records step to actually retrieve and use the needed field value.

question: An admin builds a Lightning Record Page with Dynamic Forms, placing the 'Discount_Approved__c' field with a visibility rule: show only when Amount__c > 50000. A user with 'Read Only' Field-Level Security on Discount_Approved__c meets that condition. What do they see?
options: The field is fully editable since Dynamic Forms visibility rules override Field-Level Security
The field, if shown per the visibility rule, still respects the underlying Field-Level Security
The field is completely hidden regardless of the visibility rule, because Read-Only FLS suppresses Dynamic Forms fields entirely
The user sees an error because Read-Only fields cannot be placed in Dynamic Forms at all
explanation: The trap is assuming a Lightning page-level visibility mechanism overrides a platform-wide security restriction. Dynamic Forms visibility rules only control display conditions; Field-Level Security is enforced independently and always wins for editability.

question: A company has two Page Layouts for Case ('Standard Case Layout' and 'Escalated Case Layout') assigned by profile. They migrate to Dynamic Forms, converting the Lightning Record Page to use individual field components instead of the layout-driven Details component. What happens to the original two Page Layouts?
options: They are automatically deleted once Dynamic Forms is enabled
The Page Layouts still exist and continue to control certain layout-dependent elements (like Related Lists placement in Classic
They become read-only historical records with no functional purpose whatsoever
They automatically merge into a single unified layout
explanation: The trap is assuming a full switch to Dynamic Forms makes Page Layouts entirely irrelevant. Page Layouts still govern certain other aspects (like related lists in some contexts, or serving as a fallback), so understanding what Dynamic Forms does and doesn't fully replace is a frequently tested nuance.

question: An admin wants a component visibility rule on a Lightning App Builder page to hide a 'Renewal Alert' component unless the current user has a specific Permission Set assigned, regardless of what field values the record has. Is this achievable via standard Component Visibility filters?
options: No, Component Visibility filters can only reference record field values, never user attributes like Permission Sets or Profile
Yes — Component Visibility filters can reference User fields
No, this always requires an Apex-based visibility check inside a custom Lightning Web Component
Yes, but only for Global Actions, never for standard page components
explanation: The trap is under-selling what Component Visibility filters can check. Beyond record fields, filters can reference user-context attributes, including custom permissions (often tied to Permission Set assignment), enabling permission-based visibility without any code.

question: A Compact Layout is assigned per Record Type on Opportunity. A user creates an Opportunity with Record Type 'Standard,' then later changes the Record Type to 'Partner.' What happens to the Highlights Panel display?
options: It permanently retains the 'Standard' Compact Layout since Compact Layout is fixed at record creation
The Highlights Panel updates to reflect the Compact Layout assigned to the NEW Record Type ('Partner')
Compact Layouts cannot be assigned per Record Type, only per Profile
The Highlights Panel disappears entirely whenever Record Type changes
explanation: The trap is assuming UI configuration like Compact Layout is 'locked in' at record creation. It's dynamically evaluated based on the record's current state (Record Type), so changing the Record Type later correctly changes which Compact Layout is displayed.

question: A Global Value Set 'Priority Levels' is used by picklist fields on three different objects: Case, Task, and a custom object 'Ticket.' The admin needs the Case-specific picklist to have one additional value not applicable to Task or Ticket. What is the correct approach?
options: Add the new value directly to the Global Value Set, since it will automatically apply everywhere with no side effects
Restrict the new value's availability to Case only by using picklist value restrictions at the FIELD level (available values / active values) on the Case field specifically
Create a brand new, entirely separate Global Value Set just for this one extra value
This isn't possible; each object using a Global Value Set must have IDENTICAL available values with no per-object variation
explanation: The trap is either polluting the shared Global Value Set (making the new value incorrectly available everywhere) or assuming no per-object variation is possible. Fields based on a Global Value Set CAN restrict which of the shared values are actually active/available for that specific field, allowing controlled per-object variation.

question: A 'Log a Call' Global Quick Action is added to the Salesforce mobile app's navigation menu. A rep taps it while viewing an Account record detail page. What should the App Builder expect regarding the WhatId/relationship of the resulting Task?
options: It will always automatically relate the resulting Task to the Account being viewed, with no configuration required, because Global Actions are context-aware by default in every scenario
Global Actions are NOT automatically context-aware
It will fail entirely since Global Actions cannot be used from a record's detail page
It will relate the Task to the rep's own User record instead of the Account
explanation: The trap is assuming all actions are equally 'smart' about record context. Global Actions are explicitly NOT tied to a specific object/record context by definition — behavior around auto-relating to the viewed record depends on specific configuration and is not something to assume 'just works' the way an Object-Specific Action naturally would.

question: A custom button on Opportunity uses a URL formula referencing {!Opportunity.Id} to open an external system's page for that record. Users on the Salesforce mobile app report the button doesn't appear at all, even though it's included on the mobile-compatible Page Layout's action list. What is a likely cause?
options: Custom buttons using URL as the content source, especially those relying on certain window/JavaScript-related behaviors, have historically had limited or no support in the Salesforce mobile app compared to Lightning Experience desktop — mobile action support should be verified/tested specifically, not assumed identical to desktop
Certain custom button configurations have limited mobile support
The formula syntax {!Opportunity.Id} is invalid and must be rewritten entirely
This only happens if the button is placed above the fold on the layout
explanation: The trap is assuming desktop Lightning Experience button behavior automatically carries over identically to the mobile app. Certain custom button configurations (especially any relying on JavaScript-like execution or specific window behaviors) can have gaps in mobile support that must be explicitly tested, not assumed.

question: An Object-Specific Quick Action of type 'Update a Record' is configured with predefined field values setting Status__c = "Reviewed" with no screen shown to the user. A validation rule requires a Reason field whenever Status changes to "Reviewed." What happens when a user clicks this Quick Action?
options: The Quick Action always succeeds regardless of validation rules, since predefined-value actions bypass all validation
The Quick Action's update is still subject to the object's validation rules just like any other save
Quick Actions with predefined values are exempt from validation rules by design, specifically to allow one-click actions
This scenario is impossible to configure since predefined values cannot trigger validation rules
explanation: The trap is assuming a 'quick,' screenless action is somehow exempt from standard save-time enforcement. Validation rules apply to ANY save, including automated field updates from Quick Actions — if the predefined values don't satisfy a conditionally-required field, the save is blocked just like a manual edit would be.

question: A custom Lightning Web Component's .js-meta.xml declares only the target lightning__RecordPage. The admin later tries to add this component to a Lightning Home Page. What happens?
options: It works fine since all Lightning components support all page types by default
The component will NOT be selectable/available when building a Home Page
The admin can force it onto the Home Page using a special Setup override, bypassing the meta.xml restriction
This causes the entire Lightning App Builder to crash when opening the Home Page
explanation: The trap is assuming a component's availability is universal by default. Its meta.xml configuration file explicitly declares which page targets it supports — a component scoped only to lightning__RecordPage genuinely won't show up as an option for Home Pages until that target is added.

question: A developer builds a custom LWC exposing an @api property 'recordId' intended to auto-receive the current record's Id when placed on a Record Page. The admin adds the component to an App Page (not a Record Page) and the property comes back empty at runtime. What is the correct explanation?
options: This is a bug in the component that must be fixed by the developer regardless of context
App Pages have no inherent single record context the way Record Pages do
The recordId property name is reserved and cannot be used in any custom component
App Pages automatically substitute the current user's Id instead of a record Id
explanation: The trap is assuming any missing auto-populated value indicates a broken component. App Pages fundamentally lack a specific record context — there's no record Id to inject — so an empty recordId there is expected platform behavior, not something to 'fix' in the component.

question: A business wants a highly custom, interactive data visualization embedded directly inside a Screen Flow step, with real-time re-rendering as the user interacts with it, beyond what native Flow screen components support. What is the correct approach, and what must be configured for it to actually work inside the Flow?
options: Use a Visualforce page directly, since Flow screens can natively embed any Visualforce page with zero configuration
Build a custom LWC with the lightning__FlowScreen target and exposed attributes
This is not possible; Screen Flows can only use the fixed set of standard Flow screen components
Use an Aura component, since only Aura (not LWC) can be embedded in Flow screens
explanation: The trap is assuming any custom component or a Visualforce page can be dropped into a Flow screen with no special configuration. An LWC destined for a Flow screen specifically needs the lightning__FlowScreen target declared and correctly exposed input/output properties — a real, specific technical requirement, not a generic 'any custom UI works' assumption.

question: Which statement correctly identifies WHY a legacy Visualforce page might still need to remain in a modern Lightning Experience-only org, rather than assuming everything should be rebuilt in LWC immediately?
options: Visualforce is required for all record detail pages by platform default
Visualforce still has specific niches, such as generating certain PDF/print-formatted output
LWC cannot render any tabular data, so Visualforce must be used for all reports-like displays
Visualforce pages automatically convert to LWC without any developer effort, so there's no real decision to make
explanation: The trap is the reflexive 'always modernize everything' answer. Good App Builder judgment recognizes there are still legitimate, cost-justified reasons to retain certain Visualforce use cases (like PDF generation) rather than treating every legacy page as something that must be rebuilt immediately.

question: A Page Layout's 'Salesforce Mobile and Lightning Experience Actions' section includes 10 actions. The admin assumes the mobile app will show all 10 in the exact same order and grouping as desktop Lightning Experience. Is this assumption safe?
options: Yes, mobile and desktop are always pixel-identical in action rendering with zero differences
Not necessarily — while the underlying action configuration is largely shared
Mobile apps never show Quick Actions under any configuration
Actions must be configured entirely separately for mobile using a completely different Setup area
explanation: The trap is assuming perfect visual/behavioral parity between mobile and desktop just because the configuration source (the Page Layout's action list) is shared. Real-world mobile rendering can differ (overflow menus, condensed bars), which is why testing on the actual mobile experience matters, not just trusting the shared configuration source.

question: A Compact Layout for Opportunity lists 6 fields, prioritized for the mobile Highlights Panel. The business wants a 7th critical field (a roll-up summary) always visible on mobile without pushing off an existing field. What is the correct approach and its real constraint?
options: Simply add the 7th field; Compact Layouts have no field count limit
Compact Layouts DO have a maximum field count (a defined limit, historically up to 10 fields
Roll-up summary fields cannot be included in Compact Layouts under any circumstances
This requires deleting one of the existing 6 fields first since Compact Layouts are hard-capped at exactly 6 fields
explanation: The trap is assuming either no limit exists or an artificially low hard cap (like exactly 6). Compact Layouts do have a real maximum field count, but it's higher than 6 — the more nuanced, testable point is understanding that field prominence can still vary by device even within that limit, not just the raw cap number.

question: An admin wants different users to see entirely different sets of Lightning tabs/apps in their navigation, based on their role, without creating duplicate objects or fields. What is the correct mechanism?
options: Create a separate custom object per role
Configure multiple Lightning Apps with distinct Navigation Items per profile
Modify Organization-Wide Defaults per role
Use Compact Layouts assigned per role
explanation: The trap is reaching for data-model-level solutions (new objects, OWD, Compact Layouts) for what is really an app-and-navigation-level configuration question. Multiple Lightning Apps with distinct Navigation Items, access-controlled via Profile/Permission Set, is the correct, purely UI-layer mechanism.

question: A 'Send for Signature' custom action needs to call a third-party e-signature REST API synchronously and immediately show the result to the user, with retry logic on transient network failures. A junior admin proposes a JavaScript custom button as the modern Lightning Experience solution. What is wrong with this recommendation?
options: JavaScript buttons are the officially recommended modern approach for exactly this use case
JavaScript buttons are a legacy Classic-era feature with limited/no reliable support in Lightning Experience
This action is impossible to build in Salesforce under any architecture
JavaScript buttons work fine in Lightning Experience but only for Contact and Lead objects
explanation: The trap is a junior admin confidently recommending a legacy pattern as if it were current best practice. JavaScript buttons are poorly supported in Lightning Experience; recognizing that the modern equivalent is a Flow/Quick Action invoking Apex (or a custom LWC) for this kind of synchronous, retry-capable callout is the correct App Builder judgment call.

question: A Lightning Record Page uses Component Visibility to hide a 'Competitor Analysis' component unless the Opportunity's StageName is 'Negotiation' or later. A user opens an Opportunity in 'Negotiation,' sees the component, then a Flow in the background automatically moves the Stage back to 'Qualification' due to a business rule. Without the user refreshing the page, what do they see?
options: The component visibility rule immediately updates the display, hiding the component the instant the background Flow changes the Stage
Component Visibility rules are evaluated at page load/render time based on the record data available then
This scenario is impossible since Flows cannot change Stage while a user is viewing the record
The component becomes permanently visible regardless of future Stage changes once shown once
explanation: The trap is assuming UI visibility rules behave like a live, continuously-reactive data binding to any backend change. In practice, without an explicit refresh or re-render trigger, a component's visibility reflects the record data as of page load, not necessarily a background change made moments later.

question: An admin needs a picklist field's available values to differ depending on the value of ANOTHER picklist field on the same record (e.g., 'City' options depend on the selected 'State'). Which native feature is designed for this?
options: Global Value Sets alone, with no additional configuration
Field Dependencies between the controlling and dependent picklists
Component Visibility Rules on the Lightning page
Dynamic Forms conditional visibility on the field component
explanation: The trap is reaching for page-layer tools (Component Visibility, Dynamic Forms visibility) which control WHETHER a field/component shows, not filtering WHICH VALUES are available within a picklist. Field Dependencies is the specific, purpose-built native feature for controlling-field-to-dependent-field value filtering.

question: A Quick Action of type 'Create a Record' for a related Contact is added to the Opportunity page layout's actions. After creating the Contact via this action, the admin expected it to be automatically related to the Opportunity, but the Contact ends up with no relationship back to that Opportunity. What is the likely misconfiguration?
options: Quick Actions of type Create a Record can never pre-populate any relationship field regardless of configuration
Contact does not have a direct lookup/master-detail relationship to Opportunity in standard Salesforce data model
This is a bug that requires a Salesforce support case
Quick Actions require the related object to be a child in a Master-Detail relationship, and Contact/Opportunity doesn't qualify, so no fix is possible
explanation: The trap is assuming standard 'Create a Record' actions magically infer any desired relationship. Contact and Opportunity don't have a direct standard lookup between them (relationships go through OpportunityContactRole) — the action's predefined values must be explicitly mapped to whatever real relationship field exists, and if none exists suitable to the need, the data model itself needs addressing first.

question: An admin wants to reuse the exact same arrangement of 5 components across 40 different Record Pages for various objects, and be able to update all 40 at once if the arrangement needs to change later. Placing the same 5 components manually on each of the 40 pages was the initial approach. What is the drawback, and what alternative better serves the 'update once, apply everywhere' goal?
options: There is no drawback; manually replicating components across 40 pages is the standard, recommended practice
Manually duplicating the arrangement means any future change requires editing all 40 pages individually
Lightning App Builder pages automatically sync with each other if they contain identical components, with no extra work needed
This is only possible using Experience Cloud sites, not internal Record Pages
explanation: The trap is either not recognizing the maintenance burden of manual duplication, or assuming some non-existent auto-sync feature. The genuinely correct pattern for 'change once, apply everywhere' is encapsulating the reusable arrangement inside a single custom component that gets placed across all target pages.

question: A field is marked 'Required' at the field-level (in Setup, not via a page layout), and is also included on the mobile Compact Layout. A user attempts to save a new record via the Salesforce mobile app without populating that field. What happens?
options: Mobile app saves are exempt from field-level required enforcement
The save is blocked with a required-field error, same as desktop or API
The record saves successfully but is flagged for later correction
This only applies if the field is also marked required on the Compact Layout itself, which has its own independent required enforcement
explanation: The trap is assuming mobile might have looser enforcement, or confusing Compact Layout inclusion with actual required-field enforcement (Compact Layouts don't enforce requiredness — that's a page layout or field-definition-level concept). True field-level required attributes are enforced consistently everywhere, mobile included.

question: A developer wants their custom LWC's design attributes (exposed via meta.xml) to show a dropdown of the org's Record Types for the object the component is placed against, letting admins pick one declaratively in Lightning App Builder. Is a simple text-type design attribute sufficient for this?
options: Yes, a plain text design attribute lets admins type any value freely with equivalent usability to a dropdown
Not ideally — while a plain text attribute technically works (admin manually types a Record Type name/Id)
This is entirely impossible; design attributes cannot ever expose object-specific metadata as options
Design attributes automatically become dropdowns of Record Types whenever the component is placed on a Record Page, regardless of the attribute's declared type
explanation: The trap is assuming any design attribute automatically becomes a polished, validated dropdown. A plain text attribute is functionally different (free text entry) from a true guided selector — recognizing this distinction matters for correctly setting admin expectations about the resulting configuration experience.

question: A Lightning page uses Dynamic Forms with a field's visibility condition referencing a Roll-Up Summary field's value (e.g., show 'Escalation Notes' only if Related_Case_Count__c > 5). Is this a valid configuration?
options: No, Dynamic Forms visibility conditions can only reference simple editable fields, never calculated fields like roll-up summaries or formulas
Yes — Dynamic Forms visibility conditions can reference roll-up summary and formula field values just like any other field on the record
No, this requires a custom Lightning Web Component with Apex support
Yes, but only if the roll-up summary field is first converted into an editable Number field
explanation: The trap is assuming visibility conditions are restricted to directly-editable fields. Both formula fields and roll-up summary fields are valid, referenceable values for Dynamic Forms visibility rules, just like any standard field — a broader capability than some assume.

question: An Object-Specific Action of type 'Log a Call' is customized with a modified layout removing the 'Related To' field, since the business feels it's redundant when launched from a record's own action bar. Six months later, users complain related Tasks created via this action from the Account's related list panel of a Contact show up unassociated with the correct Account context in some edge cases. What is the likely root cause?
options: Removing a field from an action's layout has no bearing on what data gets populated when the action executes
Removing the 'Related To' field from the layout only hides it from the USER-facing screen
This is a mandatory Salesforce bug requiring a support case
Log a Call actions cannot be customized at the layout level under any circumstances
explanation: The trap is assuming that hiding a field from an action's layout has zero functional side effects beyond visual simplification. Depending on where/how the action is launched, relying on automatic context-population without explicit verification (or predefined values) can lead to inconsistent relationship population — a nuance worth testing across all the contexts where an action is exposed.

question: A company wants admins (not developers) to be able to adjust a custom LWC's display text (e.g., a banner message) without needing a code deployment every time the message changes. What is the BEST design approach for the developer to enable this?
options: Hardcode the message directly in the component's JavaScript and require a redeploy for every text change, since that's the only way to guarantee consistency
Expose the message as an @api property with a design attribute in the meta.xml (of type String)
Store the message in a Custom Label only, which cannot be exposed to LWC design attributes at all
This always requires a completely separate custom object and a Flow to update the component's text
explanation: The trap is defaulting to a code-deployment-required design (hardcoding) or an overly complex one (a dedicated object + Flow) when a simple, standard technique exists: exposing the value as a String design attribute lets admins edit it declaratively per placement without any redeploy.

question: A field's Help Text is configured in Setup to display guidance when hovering over the field label. On the Salesforce mobile app, a user reports they can't get the same hover-based help text to appear no matter what they tap. What is the correct explanation?
options: Help Text never displays on any mobile device under any configuration, so this is expected and by design with no alternative
Mobile touch interfaces don't have a direct equivalent of desktop 'hover
Help Text must be manually re-entered separately for the mobile app in a dedicated mobile-specific field
This indicates the field itself is misconfigured and Help Text needs to be disabled entirely
explanation: The trap is assuming Help Text simply doesn't work on mobile at all (untrue — it's surfaced, just via a different interaction pattern suited to touch), or that a whole separate configuration is needed. The same configured Help Text is used; only the UI trigger mechanism differs due to touch vs. hover interaction models.

question: A team plans to do 6 months of feature development in a Developer Sandbox before merging into a shared integration environment. Halfway through, they realize they need updated production data to properly test a data-dependent feature, but refreshing a Developer Sandbox would wipe all their in-progress custom metadata changes made only in that sandbox. What is the correct consideration?
options: Refreshing a sandbox never affects metadata, only data, so this is a non-issue
Refreshing ANY sandbox (including Developer) overwrites BOTH data and metadata with a fresh copy from production as of the refresh point
Developer Sandboxes cannot be refreshed under any circumstances, only Full Sandboxes can
This only affects Partial Copy Sandboxes, not Developer Sandboxes
explanation: The trap is underestimating what a 'refresh' actually resets. Refreshing any sandbox type replaces BOTH data and metadata with a snapshot from production — undeployed, in-progress work only living in that sandbox is genuinely at risk unless properly source-controlled or migrated beforehand.

question: A Partial Copy Sandbox was created using a sandbox template that includes only Accounts and Opportunities from the last 90 days. Three months later, the team wants to test a new feature involving historical Cases from 2 years ago, which aren't in this sandbox. What is the correct explanation and fix?
options: Partial Copy Sandboxes always include ALL production data regardless of the template, so this shouldn't be an issue
The Partial Copy Sandbox only contains the specific subset of data defined by its sandbox template at the time it was created/last refreshed
This requires deleting the sandbox and manually re-entering the missing historical Cases one by one
Partial Copy Sandboxes automatically sync new data from production in real time regardless of the original template scope
explanation: The trap is assuming a Partial Copy Sandbox somehow contains everything, or that it stays in perfect real-time sync with production. It reflects only what the template captured as of its last refresh — accessing data outside that scope requires either adjusting the template (and refreshing) or moving to a Full Sandbox.

question: A Full Sandbox was refreshed exactly 20 days ago. The team now urgently needs a fresh refresh to pull in a critical new production configuration for testing. Is this possible immediately?
options: Yes, Full Sandboxes can be refreshed at any time with no minimum interval
No — Full Sandboxes can only be refreshed once every 29 days
No, Full Sandboxes can never be refreshed after initial creation under any circumstances
Yes, but only if a Salesforce support case is filed to override the interval every time
explanation: The trap is either assuming unlimited refresh flexibility or assuming refreshes are entirely impossible after creation. Full Sandboxes have a specific minimum refresh interval (29 days) — hitting that limit early requires either waiting it out or using a targeted metadata deployment instead of a full refresh.

question: An Outbound Change Set is created in a Sandbox and uploaded to Production, containing a custom object, three fields, and a Flow that references those fields. The deployment fails validation with an error about a missing Record Type referenced by the Flow that wasn't included in the change set. What is the correct next step?
options: Abandon the change set and manually recreate every component directly in Production instead
Use the 'View/Add Dependencies' feature on the change set to identify the missing Record Type (and any other related dependencies) and add it to the change set
Deactivate the Flow permanently since it's clearly incompatible with change sets
Change the change set's type from Outbound to Inbound to bypass the dependency check
explanation: The trap is an overreaction (abandoning the whole change set approach or permanently deactivating a perfectly good Flow) rather than the straightforward, standard fix: change sets provide a dependency-checking feature specifically for this — use it to identify and include what's missing, then redeploy.

question: A company's Sandbox and Production orgs show different behavior for the same Flow after an Outbound Change Set deployment: the Flow works in the Sandbox but throws an error in Production. Investigation reveals a Custom Setting record that the Flow depends on exists in the Sandbox but not in Production. What does this reveal about Change Sets?
options: Change Sets always deploy configuration AND any records/data referenced by that configuration automatically
Change Sets migrate METADATA/configuration only
This indicates the change set was corrupted during upload and must be regenerated
Custom Settings are automatically excluded from any Flow's dependencies, so this scenario couldn't actually occur
explanation: The trap is not distinguishing between metadata/configuration (which Change Sets DO move) and actual records/data or configured values (like Custom Setting VALUES) which Change Sets do NOT move. Flows or other automation depending on specific setup data need that data manually created in each target org — a very real, frequently-tested change set limitation.

question: A developer created a new custom field directly in the Production org (bypassing sandbox development) to quickly fix an urgent issue. The next day, an Outbound Change Set from the Sandbox — which does NOT include that emergency field since the sandbox was never refreshed — is deployed to Production for an unrelated feature. What risk does this introduce?
options: No risk; change sets always detect and merge any production-only changes automatically
The emergency field created directly in Production now represents configuration drift not reflected in the Sandbox
This will cause the Production org to become permanently locked from further deployments
The change set deployment will automatically fail and be rejected due to the mismatch
explanation: The trap is assuming change sets have some automatic drift-detection/merge capability — they don't. Making changes directly in Production outside the normal sandbox-to-production flow creates real configuration drift that must be manually reconciled (replicate the change into the sandbox, or refresh it) to avoid future deployment conflicts.

question: A change set deployment to Production requires 75% overall Apex code coverage. The org currently sits at 78% overall coverage, but the specific Apex class being modified in this change set has only 40% coverage on its own. Will the deployment succeed?
options: No, every individual class must independently have at least 75% coverage or the deployment is blocked entirely
Potentially yes — Salesforce's coverage requirement for deployment is generally evaluated as an ORG-WIDE aggregate (at least 75% overall
Yes, because code coverage requirements only apply to brand-new classes, not modified existing ones
No, because change sets always require 100% code coverage regardless of the org-wide percentage
explanation: The trap is assuming coverage requirements work per-class rather than as an org-wide aggregate (with certain trigger-level minimums). A specific class sitting well under 75% doesn't automatically block a production deployment as long as overall aggregate requirements are satisfied — a commonly misunderstood detail.

question: An ISV distributes a Managed Package containing an Apex class marked 'global' that other customers' custom code is expected to call. In a new package version, the ISV wants to change that global method's signature (add a required parameter). What is the correct consideration?
options: Global Apex signatures in a released managed package version can be freely changed at any time with no backward compatibility concern
A released global Apex signature cannot be changed without breaking subscribers
This restriction only applies to Unmanaged Packages, not Managed Packages
Global Apex methods can always be freely deleted in any subsequent package version without consequence
explanation: The trap is underestimating the permanence of 'global' in a released managed package. Once published (non-beta), global Apex identifiers are locked for backward compatibility — the ISV must add new methods/overloads rather than break existing global signatures, a well-known and heavily tested managed package constraint.

question: A customer installs a Managed Package that includes a custom object 'Warranty__c' with several fields. The customer then wants to add THEIR OWN custom field to that packaged object for internal tracking purposes not related to the package's core function. Is this possible?
options: No, Managed Package objects are entirely locked and no additional customization is possible by the installing org
Yes, customers can add their own fields and rules to packaged objects
Yes, but only by first uninstalling and reinstalling the package with a special extensibility flag enabled
No, extending a packaged object always requires purchasing a separate developer license from the ISV
explanation: The trap is over-generalizing 'managed = fully locked.' Managed packages intentionally lock only specific vendor-defined components to protect their IP, while still generally allowing the installing org to extend packaged objects with their own additional fields, validation rules, etc. — a deliberate extensibility design, not a total lockdown.

question: A company builds an internal (not customer-facing) modular application split into 4 logical modules, each deployed as a separate Unlocked Package, with proper version control (Salesforce DX source format) driving CI/CD. A stakeholder suggests these should instead be Managed Packages 'for better protection.' Is this suggestion appropriate here?
options: Yes, Managed Packages are always strictly superior regardless of use case
Not particularly — Managed Packages are primarily valuable for protecting intellectual property when distributing to EXTERNAL customers/subscribers
No, because Unlocked Packages cannot be used with Salesforce DX or version control at all
Yes, but only because Unlocked Packages are being deprecated by Salesforce
explanation: The trap is assuming 'more locked down' is always 'better.' Managed Packages solve an IP-protection problem relevant to distributing to external, separate organizations — for purely internal modular architecture, that protection isn't the goal, and Unlocked Packages' full editability/source-driven nature make them the more fitting choice.

question: A deployment plan includes a new Validation Rule requiring 'Industry' to be populated on Account going forward, deploying directly to Production with no other steps. Immediately after deployment, thousands of existing Account records without an Industry value become impossible for any user to edit (even unrelated fields) without first fixing Industry. What planning step was missed?
options: Nothing was missed; this is expected and desirable behavior with no real downside
The deployment plan should have included a pre-deployment data remediation step (bulk-populating Industry on legacy records) and/or scoped the validation rule to exclude legacy records (e.g.
Validation rules never affect existing records regardless of configuration, so this scenario couldn't actually happen
The fix is to immediately roll back Salesforce to a previous release version
explanation: The trap is not anticipating how a new validation rule interacts with EXISTING data that predates it. A solid deployment plan proactively addresses this via either data cleanup beforehand or scoping the rule (ISNEW()/date-based conditions) so legacy records aren't suddenly locked out of all future edits.

question: A release includes changes across Apex, Flow, and Custom Metadata Types, developed by three separate teams over 6 weeks using individual Developer Sandboxes with no shared version control. Integration testing reveals the Flow deployed by Team B overwrote unrelated changes Team A had made to the same Flow, because both teams edited copies independently without merging. What underlying process gap caused this?
options: Flow inherently cannot be worked on by more than one developer ever, so this was unavoidable
The lack of a shared, version-controlled source of truth (e.g.
This is a Salesforce platform limitation with no available fix, tooling, or workaround
Change Sets would have automatically merged the two teams' conflicting changes correctly
explanation: The trap is either declaring the conflict unavoidable, blaming the platform outright, or (incorrectly) trusting Change Sets to merge conflicting concurrent edits — they don't perform true merges. The real root cause is a missing version-controlled, branch-and-merge development process, which is precisely why larger, multi-team projects need DX + Git-based workflows rather than parallel, uncoordinated sandbox edits.

question: A company deploying Apex changes to Production via an automated CI/CD pipeline (Salesforce DX) wants to skip running Apex tests during deployment 'to save time,' since the tests already passed in a prior sandbox validation. Is this a sound practice for a Production deployment specifically?
options: Yes, since the tests already passed once, re-running them in Production deployment is always redundant and safe to skip
Generally no — Salesforce enforces mandatory Apex test execution (meeting coverage thresholds) for deployments to Production specifically (this requirement doesn't apply the same way to sandboxes)
Yes, and this is exactly why 'RunSpecifiedTests' exists — to always skip all testing
No, but only because CI/CD pipelines are incompatible with Salesforce DX in general
explanation: The trap is treating a Production-specific requirement as an optional efficiency shortcut. Salesforce requires Apex test execution (with coverage thresholds) for Production deployments as a structural safeguard — it isn't simply a 'skip it if you're confident' setting, and deliberately trying to bypass it undermines deployment safety.

question: A company is planning a major UI overhaul (Dynamic Forms migration, new Lightning pages) and wants a UAT environment that gives testers a realistic, full-scale experience matching current production record volumes and configuration, ahead of a go-live in 6 weeks. Budget and storage aren't primary constraints; realism is the top priority. Which sandbox type best fits, and what scheduling constraint must be planned around?
options: A Developer Sandbox, refreshed the night before UAT begins, since 'realistic enough' data isn't actually a priority stated here
A Full Sandbox, which most closely mirrors production data and metadata volume for realistic UAT
A Partial Copy Sandbox, since it always contains 100% of production data by default with more frequent refresh flexibility
Any sandbox type works equally well since 'realism' is not actually a meaningful factor in sandbox selection
explanation: The trap is either picking a less realistic environment (Developer/Partial Copy) despite the stated priority on realism, or ignoring the very real scheduling constraint of a Full Sandbox's 29-day refresh interval, which must be planned around rather than assumed to be flexible on demand.

question: A company built a Managed Package version and wants to release it to AppExchange, but their Apex classes only have 60% test coverage overall, concentrated heavily in a few classes while others have 0%. What blocks them from uploading a releasable (non-beta) package version?
options: Nothing blocks them; test coverage is only a recommendation, never enforced for package uploads
Salesforce enforces a minimum test coverage requirement (75% overall
This can be bypassed entirely by marking the package 'Unlocked' instead of 'Managed'
This only applies to Second-Generation (2GP) packages, not First-Generation (1GP) packages
explanation: The trap is assuming coverage is merely a 'best practice suggestion' with no hard enforcement at package upload time. Similar to production deployments, releasable managed package versions have real, enforced minimum coverage requirements — insufficient coverage genuinely blocks a standard (non-Beta) release.

question: A deployment plan for a complex release recommends deploying Custom Metadata Type records via Change Set alongside the Apex/Flow changes that depend on them, reasoning that 'Change Sets move all configuration uniformly.' Is this reasoning fully correct?
options: Yes, Custom Metadata Type records behave exactly like Custom Setting values and are never included in change sets
Custom Metadata Type records can be included, unlike Custom Setting values
No, Custom Metadata Types cannot be deployed via Change Sets under any circumstances and always require Apex data loading scripts
Yes, and this reasoning applies equally to actual sObject records like Accounts or Contacts too, which are also included in change sets
explanation: The trap is over-generalizing 'setup-like data' as a single uniform category. Custom Metadata Type records are actually includable in Change Sets (unlike Custom Setting values, which are not) — a specific, easily confused distinction that a careful deployment plan should explicitly verify rather than assume by analogy.

question: A large Outbound Change Set containing 150 components is created, but the admin wants to verify it will deploy cleanly to Production BEFORE the scheduled release window, without actually finalizing the deployment yet. What Salesforce capability supports this specific need?
options: There is no way to test a deployment without fully committing it immediately
A middleware/integration platform, not Data Loader or the Import Wizard
The admin must deploy to Production for real, then immediately roll back if there are issues
This can only be tested by manually recreating all 150 components by hand in a separate sandbox first
explanation: The trap is assuming there's no way to 'trial run' a deployment without committing to it live. Salesforce deployments (via Change Sets or DX/Metadata API) support a validate-only/check-only mode specifically for this purpose — verifying a clean deploy ahead of the real release without actually applying the changes yet.

question: A company uses a Developer Pro Sandbox for shared QA testing among 8 QA engineers, refreshing it every 5 days to stay reasonably current with production. A tester argues this should instead be a Full Sandbox 'because QA needs production-like data.' Is a Full Sandbox strictly necessary here?
options: Yes, QA can only ever be performed properly in a Full Sandbox, with no valid alternative
Not necessarily — Developer Pro Sandboxes offer more storage than standard Developer Sandboxes and support more frequent refreshes (every 5 days) than a Full Sandbox (29 days)
No, because Developer Pro Sandboxes cannot be used for QA testing under any circumstances by definition
Yes, but only because more than 5 people are using the sandbox simultaneously
explanation: The trap is an absolute claim ('QA always needs Full Sandbox') without weighing the actual tradeoffs. Developer Pro offers more capacity and faster refresh cycles than Full Sandbox — whether that's 'enough' depends on the specific QA scenario's real data-volume needs, not a blanket rule.

question: An admin wants to deploy a single custom field from a Sandbox to Production using a Change Set, but that field is referenced by a validation rule, a Flow, AND a Report Type already active in the target Production org (created independently there, not via change set). Will including just the new field (with no other components) in the Outbound Change Set succeed?
options: No, this will always fail because the field is referenced by so many existing components in Production
This can succeed — components ALREADY existing in the target org (validation rule, Flow
This requires including the validation rule, Flow, and Report Type in the change set as well, since they all reference the field
This can only work if the field is deployed as part of a Managed Package instead
explanation: The trap is assuming every referencing component elsewhere must be re-bundled into the change set. Change sets only need to carry over what's actually MISSING from the target org — components that already exist there and simply reference the new (incoming) field don't need to be re-included, since they're not what's missing.

question: A company wants to allow a specific set of trusted 'Power Users' to deploy their own vetted Flow changes directly via Change Set into Production, without going through the central admin team, to speed up minor iterations. What must be true for this delegation to work safely?
options: Change Sets have no permission model, so anyone with a Salesforce login can already do this by default
The Power Users need the 'Deploy Change Sets' permission (and the org needs deployment connections properly configured between the relevant sandbox and Production)
This requires giving Power Users full System Administrator profiles, since deployment always requires that specific profile
This is not possible; only a single designated 'Release Manager' user can ever deploy change sets in any org
explanation: The trap is either assuming no permission gating exists, or wildly over-provisioning access (full System Admin) to achieve a narrower goal. The 'Deploy Change Sets' permission specifically supports this kind of delegation without granting broader admin rights — though pairing it with process safeguards is the more complete, realistic answer.
